Chapter 6: Measures of Variability

In Chapter 5, we learned about three ways you can describe central tendency for a single variable. In this chapter, we will be focusing on a second way you can describe your variable: in terms of variability. Variability is a value that describes the dispersion or spread of values around a point of central tendency. This chapter will describe four types:

  1. Range: : Distance separating the highest from the lowest values.
  2. Sum of Squares: Squared deviation scores (which represent how far each value is from the mean) to measure overall variability.
  3. Variance: Another way to measure overall variability; it accounts for the size of your population or sample and is calculated by dividing your sum of squares by N.
  4. Standard Deviation: Another way to measure overall variability; it removes squared units (the unit of variance is squared). You take the square root of the variance to find your standard deviation.

For continuous variables, a form of variability is often reported alongside central tendency values because together, they can best describe a variable. There are no widely used measures of variability for categorical (i.e., nominal or ordinal) variables. You can still describe a nominal variable by finding a mode and looking at the representation across categories in tables (see Chapter 4). However, with continuous variables, you can report a variety of measures of variability, including range and standard deviation. These two forms are the most reported; you need to calculate the sum of squares and the variance to find your standard deviation, though, so you could report all four forms of variability.

Variability

In addition to finding the most common, middle, or average value, it is also important to evaluate the dispersion of data (i.e., the variability) around the central tendency value. For example, if your other values are tightly clustered around a measure of central tendency, you would have low variability (i.e., the values are all close together). However, if your other values are spread out around a measure of central tendency, you would have high variability  (i.e., the values are widely distributed).

If we look at the following distributions of data, both of their means are 8.

Distribution 1: 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10

Σ x = 56 N = 7

\begin{align*}
\bar{x} &= \frac{\Sigma x}{N} \\[1ex]
&= \frac{56}{7} \\[1ex]
&= 8
\end{align*}

Distribution 2: 0, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 16

Σ x = 56 N = 7

\begin{align*}
\bar{x} &= \frac{\Sigma x}{N} \\[1ex]
&= \frac{56}{7} \\[1ex]
&= 8
\end{align*}

Although their mean values are the same, the variability is different between these two distributions. Distribution 1 has low variability because most of the values are clustered around 8 (scores range from 6 to 10). Distribution 2 has high variability because the values are more spread out from the mean (scores range from 0 to 16). See Figure 6.1.

 

Figure 6.1. Two distributions with a mean of 8, but Distribution 1 has low variability, and Distribution 2 has high variability.

This chapter will focus on calculating different types of variability to help describe the dispersion of values around your point of central tendency.

Range

The first type of variability to describe your continuous variable is range. Range is a measure of variability that represents the distance separating the highest from the lowest values. To find the range, you subtract the lowest value from the highest value:

Formula 6.1. Calculating Range

Formula for range:

R a n g e = x highest − x lowest

Continuing our previous example, we can include the range to highlight the different variability between the two distributions:

Distribution 1: 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 9, 10

  • Your highest value is 10 and your lowest value is 6.
  • R a n g e = 10 −   6 = 4
  • The range would be 4.

Distribution 2: 0, 5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 16

  • Your highest value is 16 and your lowest value is 0.
  • R a n g e = 16 − 0 = 16
  • The range would be 16.

The range can be helpful to describe the spread or dispersion around the mean. For example, you could describe each distribution in terms of range:

  • Distribution 1 had a mean of 8, with a range of 4 (scores ranged from 6 to 10).
  • Distribution 2 had a mean of 8, with a range of 16 (scores ranged from 0 to 16).

So, the range can be useful when describing and comparing these two distributions. Again, although they had the same mean, Distribution 1 had low variability (range = 4) compared with Distribution 2, which had higher variability (range = 16).

Sum of Squares

Another measure of variability is the sum of squares, which uses squared deviation scores to measure overall variability. Deviation scores tell you how far away each value is from the mean; you can see how little or how much the scores deviate from the mean. We will walk through an example to help illustrate deviation scores and how to calculate the sum of squares.

Example: Describing the Age of Children in Foster Care Using the Sum of Squares

For this example, a social worker is examining the age of children who were placed in foster care this quarter. From her case files, she pulls out the following information, which includes the individual ages for each child and the average age: 4, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 16

Σ x = 52 N = 8

\begin{align*}
\bar{x} &= \frac{\Sigma x}{N} \\[1ex]
&= \frac{52}{8} \\[1ex]
&= 6.5
\end{align*}

To find the sum of squares as a measure of variability, we’ll need to see how far each of these eight age scores is from the mean of 6.5. We’ll do this by calculating eight deviation scores. To help organize the calculation of deviation scores, we’ll use Table 6.1. Some notes for using this table are as follows:

  • Each row represents a child.
  • The first column identifies the child.
  • The second column is the value for each child’s age (e.g., child 1 was age 4, so x = 4
  • The third column is the sample mean ( x ¯ x x ¯
  • The fourth column is where we will calculate the deviation score for each child. The equation is listed at the top of this column ( ( x – x ¯ ) x
Table 6.1. Calculating Deviation Scores
Child x x ¯ ( x – x ¯ )
1 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5
2 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5
3 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5
4 5 6.5 (5 − 6.5) = −1.5
5 6 6.5 (6 − 6.5) = −0.5
6 6 6.5 (6 − 6.5) = −0.5
7 7 6.5 (7 − 6.5) = 0.5
8 16 6.5 (16 − 6.5) = 9.5
  • Now that we have our deviation scores, let’s try adding them together. Whenever you add deviation scores, you will always get zero. This is because your deviation scores are balanced around your central tendency or mean. In our example, the sum of deviation scores below the mean (i.e., the negative deviation scores) totals −10. The sum of deviation scores above the mean (i.e., the positive deviation scores) totals 10. Thus, these balance each other out–they zero each other out. See Figure 6.2.
Figure 6.2. Deviation scores are balanced around the mean.

So, because zero is not a meaningful measure of variability, you’ll need to square each of your deviation scores. Squaring your deviation scores will get rid of negative numbers and allow you to have a meaningful value to measure variability across deviation scores. Let’s add a column to our table so that we can square our deviation scores (see Table 6.2). The equation is listed at the top of this column. We will take the deviation score from the fourth column and square it. For Child 1, we would take their deviation score of −2.5 and square it. So, the squared deviation score for Child 1 is 6.25. You will do this for every row to find the squared deviation score for each child.

You’ll also notice a new row at the bottom, where we can include summary information for the table. We’ll use these numbers throughout other calculations of variability, so they can be useful to include.

  • Column 1 summary: N = 8 means that we have 8 total children in this sample.
  • Column 2 summary: Sum of x (i.e., adding all the x values together). This is used when calculating the mean of the sample. In this example, we took the sum of x (which was 52) and divided it by 8. This gave us the mean of 6.5.
  • Column 3 summary: The sample mean is 6.5.
  • Column 4 summary: To double check that you calculated your deviation scores correctly, this reminds you to sum your deviation scores. You will always get a value of 0 here.
  • Column 5 summary: To finally get your sum of squares value, you’ll add all of your squared deviation scores. This is why we call it the “sum of squares”–we are summing all of the squared deviation scores to obtain a value to represent the amount of variability in this data set.
Table 6.2. Calculating Squared Deviation Scores and Summary Information (Bottom Row)
Child x x ¯ ( x – x ¯ ) ( x – x ¯ ) 2
1 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5 (−2.5)2  = 6.25
2 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5 (−2.5)2  = 6.25
3 4 6.5 (4 − 6.5) = −2.5 (−2.5)2  = 6.25
4 5 6.5 (5 − 6.5) = −1.5 (−1.5)2  = 2.25
5 6 6.5 (6 − 6.5) = −0.5 (−0.5)2  = 0.25
6 6 6.5 (6 − 6.5) = −0.5 (−0.5)2  = 0.25
7 7 6.5 (7 − 6.5) = 0.5 (0.5)2  = 0.25
8 16 6.5 (16 − 6.5) = 9.5 (9.5)2  = 90.25
N = 8 Σ x = 52 x ¯ = 6.5 Σ ( x – x ¯ ) = 0 Σ ( x – x ¯ ) 2 = 112

Thus, after calculating deviation scores, then squaring those deviation scores, you sum all of those scores to find your sum of squares value. In this example, the sum of squares is 112. There are several ways you can note this:

S S x = 112

Σ ( x – x ¯ ) 2 = 112

The equation for the sum of squares ( Σ ( x – x ¯ ) 2  is also known as the definitional formula, because you are taking the sum of squares of your deviation scores.

Formula 6.2. Definitional formula for sum of squares

S S x = Σ ( x – x ¯ ) 2

There is another method for calculating the sum of squares that doesn’t involve the need to calculate deviation scores for every participant. It can also help reduce the likelihood of rounding errors. This equation for the sum of squares is referred to as the computational formula. 

Formula 6.3. Computational formula for sum of squares

S S x = ∑ x 2 − ( ∑ x ) 2 N

If we continue with our same example from this chapter, you already have two pieces of this equation from when you calculated the mean (also in the bottom row of the table). A table can be helpful to organize this information, but you are only calculating one column this time (see Table 6.3). In the third column, you’ll take each child’s age ( x x 2

Table 6.3. Squared x Values and Summary Information (Bottom Row) for Sum of Squares Computational Formula
Child x x 2
1 4 42 = 16
2 4 42 = 16
3 4 42 = 16
4 5 52 = 25
5 6 62 = 36
6 6 62 = 36
7 7 72 = 49
8 16 162 = 256
N = 8 Σ x = 52 ∑ x 2 = 450

You now have all the values you need (pulling from the bottom row of the table) to calculate the sum of squares using the computation formula.

Example 6.1. Computational Formula for Sum of Squares

Computational formula for sum of squares:

S S x = ∑ x 2 − ( ∑ x ) 2 N

Our example: 

S S x a m p ; = 450 − ( 52 ) 2 8 S S x a m p ; = 450 − 2704 8 S S x a m p ; = 450 − 338 S S x a m p ; = 112

So, we find that the sum of squares is 112. This number might seem familiar to you; that’s because we found this exact value for the sum of squares using the definitional formula for the sum of squares. Again, we can notate our sum of squares of x

S S x = 112

Variance

Now that we have calculated the sum of squares, we have an estimate of the amount of variability in our sample. However, the sum of squares is sensitive to the size of the sample (or population). The larger your sample or population size (N), the greater your sum of squares value will be. This is because you have more data and thus more deviation scores to square. So, the spread of data or variability has not increased, but the size of your N has. Variance is another way to measure overall variability, but it accounts for the size of your population or sample, by dividing your sum of squares value by N.

You’ll notice that the equations for variance have different symbols, and their denominators are different. Our population equation for variance includes the lowercase Greek letter, σ s

Formula 6.4. Variance Formulas

Population variance:

σ 2 = S S x N

Sample variance:

s 2 = S S x ( N − 1 )

Whereas the population calculation for variance divides your sum of squares value by N ( N – 1 ) N accounts for degrees of freedom. The definition and reasons for using degrees of freedom are discussed in Chapter 14 (i.e., when using an estimate from a sample to make estimates about a population, you lose a degree of freedom).

Example: Describing the Age of Children in Foster Care Using the Variance

We previously found the sum of squares for our sample of eight children (112). If we want to calculate our variance, we’ll use our sample equation for variance:

Example 6.2. Calculating Sample Variance

Formula for sample variance:

s 2 = S S x ( N − 1 )

Our example:

s 2 = 112 ( 8 − 1 ) = 112 7 = 16

Just for practice, let’s use the same sum of squares and number of children, but let’s pretend we are working with a population. Let’s calculate the variance for a population.

Example 6.3. Calculating Population Variance

Formula for population variance:

σ 2 = S S x N

Our example:

σ 2 = 112 8 = 14

The adjustment we make for degrees of freedom with the sample variance gives us a more conservative estimate of variability ( s 2 = 16 σ 2 = 14

Standard Deviation

Our final type of variability is called the standard deviation. This variability value is the most reported type of variability for continuous variables, mainly because we do not usually speak in squared units (i.e., variance estimates use sum of squares estimates, so they are the averages of squared values). Therefore, the standard deviation is another way to measure overall variability, but it removes squared units. You’ll take the square root of the variance to find your standard deviation.

Formula 6.5. Formulas for Standard Deviation

Population standard deviation:

σ = σ 2

Sample standard deviation:

s = s 2

Example: Describing the Age of Children in Foster Care Using the Standard Deviation

We have two variance estimates in the previous example, so let’s calculate a standard deviation for the sample and the population.

First, let’s find the standard deviation for the variance from a sample.

Example 6.4. Sample Standard Deviation

Formula for sample standard deviation:

s = s 2

Our example: 

s a m p ; = 16 s a m p ; = 4

Next, let’s find the standard deviation for the variance from a population.

Example 6.5. Population Standard Deviation

Formula for population standard deviation:

σ = σ 2

Our example: 

σ a m p ; = 14 σ a m p ; = 3.74

We finally have our final forms of variability: The standard deviation for our sample is 4, and the standard deviation for our population is 3.74. As you’ll see in Chapter 7, we’ll use the standard deviation to visualize what this amount of variability looks like around the mean.

Summary

In this chapter, we learned about different measures of variability for continuous variables, including the range, sum of squares, variance, and standard deviation. We learned new symbols and equations for these calculations. Although symbols look different depending whether you have a population or a sample, the equations stay the same, except for the equation for variance. Remember, your denominator for variance is different for a population (N) versus a sample (N – 1). Table 6.4 summarizes the equations covered in this chapter.

Table 6.4. Summary Table of Chapter Equations for Populations and Samples
Concept Population Parameters Sample Statistics
Mean μ = ∑ x N x ¯ = ∑ x n
Deviation score ( x – μ ) ( x – x ¯ )
Sum of squares (definitional) S S x = Σ ( x – μ ) 2 S S x = Σ ( x – x ¯ ) 2
Sum of squares (computational) S S x = ∑ x 2 − ( ∑ x ) 2 N S S x = ∑ x 2 − ( ∑ x ) 2 N
Variance σ 2 = S S x N s 2 = S S x ( N − 1 )
Standard deviation σ = σ 2 s = s 2

Chapter 7: Distributions and Their Shapes

When describing univariate parameters and statistics, we have examined ways to describe central tendency (Chapter 5) and variability (Chapter 6). In this chapter, we will be focusing on the third way you can describe a continuous variable: by examining distributions and the shapes of these distributions. As we learned in Chapter 6, there are no measures of variability for categorical variables, so the focus of this chapter and its distributions will be working with continuous variables. A distribution is the way in which values in a data set are organized and dispersed. Distributions can be visualized with graphs, which also help display different distributional shapes. This chapter will examine the following concepts:

  • The Normal Distribution: Also referred to as a bell-shaped curve because of its shape, the normal distribution is a theoretical distribution. This means that the distribution resulted from mathematical principles rather than actual data. Thus, it provides a visual and key features of how a variable is expected to look (i.e., be distributed). In statistics, we can use this theoretical model and compare our actual data distributions to it; we can approximate it.
  • Kurtosis: Kurtosis assesses the “peakedness” of a distribution, which reflects the weight of the distribution tails.
  • Skew: Skew is the amount by which a distribution departs from being symmetrical, pulled by outliers on one side of a distribution.

Distributions

As noted, a distribution is the way in which values in a dataset are organized and dispersed. We can plot our scores (x) to see our distribution with graphs, which can help us display different distributional shapes.

The Normal Distribution

Also referred to as the bell-shaped curve because of its shape, the normal distribution is a theoretical distribution (see Figure 7.4). This means that the distribution resulted from mathematical principles, rather than actual data. Thus, it provides a visual showing the key features of how a variable is expected to look (i.e., be distributed). In statistics, we can use this theoretical model and compare our actual data distributions to it; we can approximate it.

Figure 7.4. The Normal Distribution.

Most data points cluster around the mean, and the rest taper off on either side of the high point of the curve. As you get farther away from the mean, you have the upper and lower tails of the distribution. There are three key features of the normal distribution:

1. The mean, median, and mode are all the same value at the center, the high point of the distribution.

2. It is symmetrical; if you folded the distribution in half, you’d have mirror images. 50% of the distribution is below the mean, median, and mode, and 50% of the distribution is above the mean, median, and mode (see Figure 7.5).

Figure 7.5. The mean, median, and mode shown at the center, at the high point of the curve. The normal distribution is symmetrical, so 50% of the distribution falls on each side.

3. Approximately 68.27% of scores are located within 1 standard deviation below and above the mean (see Figure 7.6), 95.45% of scores are within 2 standard deviations below and above the mean (see Figure 7.7), and 99.73% of scores are within 3 standard deviations below and above the mean (see Figure 7.8).

Figure 7.6. Approximately 68.27% of scores are located within 1 standard deviation of the mean.
Figure 7.7. Approximately 95.45% of scores are located within 2 standard deviations of the mean.
Figure 7.8. Approximately 99.73% of scores are located within 3 standard deviations of the mean.

Based on these three key features, we can use this distribution to help us understand approximately where data points are located. As shown earlier, the mean (and median and mode) is at the center line of the distribution. The distribution is symmetrical in shape. In Figure 7.9, standard deviations are used to help measure the amount of variability around the mean. There are three lines above the mean, which represent 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations above the mean. There are also three lines below the mean, which represent 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations below the mean. We can use our mean and standard deviation to calculate exactly what those lines represent. This also helps us understand where proportions of scores fall on this distribution.

Figure 7.9. Normal distribution with standard deviation lines.

We can calculate exactly what the line values represent for any given problem, but the normal distribution helps us understand that approximately 68.27% of scores fall under the highest part of the curve, within 1 standard deviation on either side of the mean (see Figure 7.10). The second key feature is that the distribution is symmetrical, so you have half of the total area (34.135%) below the mean, and half of the total area (34.135%) is above the mean.

As you go out to 2 standard deviations from the mean, you are now seeing that approximately 95.45% of scores fall in this area. Again, this is symmetrical, so 47.725% is below the mean, and 47.725% of scores are above the mean.

Finally, as you go out to 3 standard deviations from the mean, you are now seeing that approximately 99.73% of scores are in this area of the distribution (49.865% below the mean, 49.865% above the mean).

Figure 7.10. Normal distribution with standard deviation lines and areas shown.

Using the Mean and Standard Deviation on the Normal Distribution

Once we calculate the mean and standard deviation for a population or sample, we can use these values to visualize our distributions. Let’s use our example from earlier in the chapter: mean ( x ¯ = 8 s = 1.83 μ σ

Figure 7.11. Normal distribution with sample notation.
Figure 7.12. Normal distribution with population notation.

First, let’s find 1 standard deviation below the mean: 8 – 1.83 = 6.17. Then let’s find 1 standard deviation above the mean: 8 + 1.83 = 9.83. This means that 68.27% of scores fall between 6.17 and 9.83.

  • Mean – 1 standard deviation: 8 – 1.83 = 6.17.
  • Mean + 1 standard deviation: 8 + 1.83 = 9.83.

You’ll do the same process to calculate 2 and 3 standard deviations from the mean:

  • Mean – 2 standard deviations: 8 – 1.83(2)= 4.34.
  • Mean + 2 standard deviations: 8 + 1.83(2) = 11.66.
  • Mean – 3 standard deviations: 8 – 1.83(3) = 2.51.
  • Mean + 3 standard deviations: 8 + 1.83(3) = 13.49.

From this information, you know that 68.26% of scores fall between 6.17 and 9.83, 95.45% of scores fall between 4.34 and 11.66, and 99.73% of scores fall between 2.51 and 13.49 (see Figure 7.13).

Figure 7.13. Normal distribution with mean and standard deviation values for our example.

We can also use our example from Chapters 5 and 6 to visualize the mean and standard deviation for the sample that completed the cognitive decline assessment. The mean ( x ¯ = 79.69 s = 13.14

  • Mean – 1 standard deviation: 79.69 – 13.14 = 66.55.
  • Mean + 1 standard deviation: 79.69 + 13.14 = 92.83.
  • Mean – 2 standard deviations: 79.69 – 13.14 (2) = 53.41.
  • Mean + 2 standard deviations: 79.69 + 13.14 (2) = 105.97.
  • Mean – 3 standard deviations: 79.69 – 13.14 (3) = 40.27.
  • Mean + 3 standard deviations: 79.69 + 13.14 (3) = 119.11.

From this information, you now know that 68.27% of scores fall between 66.55 and 92.83, 95.45% of scores fall between 53.41 and 105.97, and 99.73% of scores fall between 40.27 and 119.11 (see Figure 7.14).

Figure 7.14. Normal distribution with mean and standard deviation labeled for our second example.

Common Applications in Social Work

Calculating univariate, descriptive statistics, and using distributions to visualize continuous variables can be helpful to social workers. One common example is when we use standardized assessments. These structured tools have gone through rigorous research, with a systematic or uniform method of administration and scoring. Often, standardized assessments include information about what is called a general norm sample. The researchers who created the assessment administered it with a large, representative sample of people. Then, from this research, they determined a general normal sample mean or average score for the assessment, as well as a standard deviation, or the amount of variability in this sample. This information is provided to clinicians so that they can then compare their client or group of clients to the general norm sample mean and standard deviation.

Example: Plotting Client Scores with Standardized Assessments

Imagine we use a standardized assessment of anxiety for our clients; the scoring manual provides the following information:

  • Mean = 50.
  • Standard deviation = 12.
  • Interpretation information: If clients have a score that is more than 2 standard deviations above the mean, their scores are considered clinically significant. If they fall between 1 and 2 standard deviations above the mean, then their symptoms are considered “elevated.”
  • So, if clients score higher than 74, they are clinically significant scores, and if clients score between 62 and 74, they have elevated scores.

You have four clients take the assessment, and their scores are as follows: Jhmira scores a 47, Rodney scores a 59, Sarah scores a 68, and Lupita scores an 84. Figure 7.15  shows where their scores fall in relation to the normal distribution of the general norm sample (the mean is plotted at 50).

Figure 7.15. Four client scores plotted on a normal distribution.

Using this general norm sample’s normal distribution from the scoring manual, you can then determine the following about your clients:

  • Jhmira and Rodney do not have elevated or clinically significant symptoms.
  • Sarah has elevated symptoms.
  • Lupita has clinically significant symptoms.

Shapes of Distributions

Distributions of data can vary, which can affect their shape. Although we can approximate the normal distribution (which can be helpful for understanding where proportions of scores fall based on the key features of the normal distribution), we do not always have data that resemble the normal distribution. Thus, we have to examine the shapes of our distributions to assess for issues of kurtosis and skew. This book briefly describes how kurtosis and skew, two descriptive statistics, can help describe the shape of a distribution.

Kurtosis assesses the “peakedness” of a distribution, which reflects the weight of the distribution’s tails. A normal distribution has a mesokurtic shape. When a distribution has high levels of kurtosis, known as aleptokurtic shape, there are more extreme outliers that extend the tail regions. This makes the tail regions longer and flatter. The center is also more peaked from a greater concentration of data points close to the mean (almost like you’re pinching and pulling up on the top of the distribution).

When a distribution has low levels of kurtosis, known as a platykurtic shape, it has fewer cases in the tails. These distributions have fewer outliers, and data points are more evenly distributed around the center of the distribution (i.e., data points are less likely to deviate too far from the mean). This means there is lower consistency, and it makes the center almost flattened and broad in shape (almost like you’re flattening the distribution). Figure 7.16 shows these three types of kurtosis.

Figure 7.16. Distributional shapes in terms of kurtosis.

With more advanced statistical analyses, checking the amount of kurtosis is an important data-checking step. A mesokurtic shape is ideal for many statistical analyses.

Skew is the amount to which a distribution departs from being symmetrical, pulled by outliers on one side of a distribution. A normal distribution has zero skew because it is perfectly symmetrical.

Distributions are positively skewed when outliers exist on the right side of the distribution; the distributional shape tries to account for these outliers, which stretches the tail on the right side. This leaves the rest of the distribution, including the curve and tail on the left side to be clustered.

Distributions are negatively skewed when outliers exist on the left side of the distribution; the distributional shape tries to account for these outliers, which stretches the tail on the left side. This leaves the rest of the distribution, including the curve and tail on the right side to be clustered.

In both cases of positive and negative skew, the mean is affected by the skew; it is pulled higher (with positive skew) or lower (with negative skew) to account for the outliers (see Figure 7.17). Thus, not only is the distributional shape no longer symmetrical, but the mean is also no longer at the top, the center of the distribution.

Figure 7.17. Negative and positive skew.

Other Shapes

Finally, there are other shapes that distributions can take, including uniform and bimodal distributions. A uniform distribution (sometimes called a flat distribution) is when every value of a distribution has the same frequency or very similar frequencies. These distributions are rectangular in shape (see Figure 7.18).

Figure 7.18. Example of a uniform distribution.

Bimodal distributions have two points at which values cluster; that is, they have two modes (see Figure 7.19).

Figure 7.19. Example of a bimodal distribution.

Summary

This chapter highlighted visualizations of how values in a dataset are organized and dispersed. These graphs can help assess for a normal distribution shape and show whether there are concerns with kurtosis or skew. You can also assess for a uniform or bimodal distribution. However, if you have a shape that resembles the normal distribution, you can plot the mean and standard deviation. This visualization can be helpful when using standardized assessments and comparing client scores to standard norm scores. Also, we will return to the importance of the normal distribution shape in Chapter 11 because the normal shape is used in an array of inferential statistics.

As a recap, our normal distribution has three key features:

  • The mean, median, and mode are all the same value at the center, the high point of the distribution.
  • It is symmetrical; if you folded the distribution in half, you’d have mirror images; 50% of the distribution is below the mean, median, and mode, and 50% of the distribution is above the mean, median, and mode.
  • Approximately 68.27% of scores are located within 1 standard deviation below and above the mean, 95.45% of scores are within 2 standard deviations below and above the mean, and 99.73% of scores are within 3 standard deviations below and above the mean.

III

Unit 3. Standard Normal Distribution and z-Scores

This next section will illustrate how we can standardize our variables, which will allow for comparisons and answer questions about probability.

8

Chapter 8: The Standard Normal Distribution and z-Scores

Standardization

In Chapter 7, we saw that the normal distribution has key features of central tendency and a symmetrical shape, and we also saw where the scores are located (e.g., approximately 68.27% of scores are located within 1 standard deviation below and above the mean, 95.45% of scores are within 2 standard deviations below and above the mean, and 99.73% of scores are within 3 standard deviations below and above the mean). Most inferential statistics are built on the assumption that data are normally distributed, so we have to check for outliers that may skew our distributions or show leptokurtic or platykurtic shapes. We’ll proceed in this book under the assumption that we have checked for these deviations, and we’ll be working with normally distributed data.

Depending on whether we have a population or a sample, we can use our mean and standard deviation as guidelines for plotting information on a normal distribution. This can be a helpful visual representation, especially if you are using assessment tools that provide information on a general norm sample. This allows you to see how your client or participant scores in relation to this sample.

However, what if we want to compare variables that are on different scales? Or what if we want to compare the same variable across different samples or populations? In these cases, we can standardize our scores so that they all use the same scaling.

Example: Referrals Using Different Standardized Assessments for Generalized Anxiety Disorder

A private practice is starting a group treatment program for generalized anxiety disorder. Participants will be selected for treatment based on their anxiety screening assessment scores. Referral sources use a variety of different anxiety assessments, so the practice needs to find a way to standardize across these different assessments to compare potential participants.

For this example and anytime you want to convert scores on the same scale, you can standardize raw scores (from their original scoring) into standard scores. This allows you to compare variables that are on different scales, or variables that come from different samples or populations. We can calculate standard scores so that we can compare scores using the same scaling.

Let’s say the practitioners want to compare Potential Participant 1 to Potential Participant 2. Here’s their information:

  • Potential Participant 1:
    • Raw Score: 78
    • Standardized Assessment: General norm sample mean is 70, and standard deviation is 10.
  • Potential Participant 2:
    • Raw Score: 66
    • Standardized Assessment: General norm sample mean is 50, and standard deviation is 12.

We can use z-scores and the standard normal distribution to standardize their scores and help us make an informed decision.

Figure 8.1 “People in a Psychotherapy Session” by Antoni Shkraba Studio, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

Standard Normal Distribution and z-Scores

In the process of converting our raw scores to z-scores, we will be plotting our z-scores on the standard normal distribution. The standard normal distribution has a mean of 0 (at the center of the distribution), and a standard deviation of 1 (lines going above and below the mean at the center of the distribution are in increments of 1) (see Figure 8.2). Thus, if a z-score is positive, it is above the mean (of 0). If a z-score is negative, it is below the mean (of 0). Thus, you can transform any raw scores into z-scores, plot them on the standard normal distribution, and then easily make comparisons because they are on the same standard scale.

Figure 8.2. The standard normal distribution.

To compute a z-score for an individual, you will need to know the population or sample mean and standard deviation (often provided to you in assessment guides, scoring manuals, research articles, etc.). Because you are using the standard normal distribution (which is scaled in terms of standard deviations), the z-score represents the number of standard deviations that a score is from the mean. Thus, you need three pieces of information for the equation:

  • Raw score (x): This is the score that you want to convert.
  • Population or sample mean (𝜇 or x̅): this is the mean of the group you are comparing your participant’s score to.
  • Population or sample standard deviation (𝜎 or s): This is the standard deviation of the group you are comparing your participant’s score to.

Formula 8.1. Calculating z-score

Formula for z-score (population):

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Formula for z-score (sample): 

z = ( x − x ¯ ) s

So, in following the order of operations, you’ll first subtract within the parentheses: Take the raw score minus the population or sample mean. Next, you’ll take that difference and divide by the population or sample standard deviation.

Key points about these calculations are as follows:

  • z-Scores can be positive or negative.
    • Positive z-scores are above the mean of 0.
    • Negative z-scores are below the mean of 0.
  • z-Scores can be 0 (if the raw score is the same value as the population or sample mean).

So, if an individual has a z-score of 1.5, they are 1.5 standard deviations above the mean. If they have a z-score of -0.75, they are 0.75 standard deviations below the mean.

Going back to our example, we can standardize our two potential participants’ anxiety assessment scores:

  • Potential Participant 1:
    • Raw Score: 78
    • The general norm mean is 70, and the standard deviation is 10.

Example 8.1. Finding z-Score for Participant 1

Formula for z-score: 

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example: 

z = ( 78 − 70 ) 10 = 0.80

Their z-score is 0.80, so we know that this score is above the mean (i.e., it’s a positive score).

  • Potential Participant 2:
    • Raw Score: 66
    • The general norm mean is 50, and the standard deviation is 12.

Example 8.2. Finding z-Score for Participant 2

Formula for z-score:

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example: 

z = ( 66 − 50 ) 12 = 1.33

Their z-score is 1.33, so we know that this score is also above the mean (i.e., it’s a positive score), and it is higher than Potential Participant 1’s score.

We can then plot both of their z-scores on the standard normal distribution (see Figure 8.3). From this comparison, we can see that Potential Participant 2 has a higher anxiety score, so this individual will likely get the next spot in the group treatment program.

Figure 8.3. Standard normal distribution with two potential participant’s z-scores labeled.

Example: Multiple Assessments for the Same Person

Another time z-scores can be helpful is when you have multiple assessments for the same person. For example, you may have a client complete an anxiety assessment and a depression assessment. You can take their scores, even if they are on different assessments with their own scaling systems, and convert them into z-scores. This will allow you to visualize an array of scores for one client all on one visual for a more comprehensive understanding.

Let’s say your client, Sally, completed an anxiety assessment and a depression assessment. From each scoring manual, you pull out the following information:

  • Anxiety: x = 75, x̅ = 70, s = 10
  • Depression: x = 85, x̅ = 90, s = 10

You’ll then calculate Sally’s two z-scores and plot them on the standard normal distribution.

Example 8.3. Calculating z-Scores for Multiple Assessments

Formula for z-score:

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example:

Anxiety

z = ( 75 − 70 ) 10 = 0.50

Depression

z = ( 85 − 90 ) 10 = − 0.50

From these calculations, we can see that Sally’s anxiety score is 0.50 standard deviations above the mean, whereas her depression score is 0.50 standard deviations below the mean (see Figure 8.4). This information may help prioritize addressing her anxiety symptoms, given the higher z-score relative to her depression score.

Figure 8.4. Using the standard normal distribution to compare across assessments.

Interpreting z-Scores: Areas Under the Standard Normal Distribution Curve

z-Scores can be further interpreted in terms of proportion (e.g., describe the proportion or percentage of a group with a certain attribute) and probability (e.g., predict the probability or likelihood that someone may obtain a particular score); you can use Table A.1 in the Appendix to look up areas between your z-score and the mean, as well as the area beyond your z-score. These areas can be used to describe the proportion of a population with scores less than a particular z-score, or probability (e.g., what is the probability of scoring higher than a positive z-score?).

After you calculate someone’s z-score, you can use Table A.1 to learn more about their score. For example, you may be curious about what percentage of people scored higher than your client’s z-score or what percentage of people scored between the mean and your client’s z-score. Table A.1 allows you to look up a z-score and understand what proportion of people’s scores fell in a particular area of the distribution.

To use Table A.1, first, you’ll calculate your z-score. Then, you’ll find that z-score in the first column of the table. In that row, you have two additional pieces of information: (1) In the second column, you’ll find the proportion of scores that fall between the mean (of 0) and that z-score. This is known as the area between mean and z (pictured in red in Figure 8.5). (2) In the third column, you’ll find the proportion of scores that fall beyond the z-score, known as the area beyond z (pictured in blue in Figure 8.5).

Figure 8.5. Using z-scores to assess areas under the standard normal distribution.

For example, if we look up a z-score of 1.00, we see that the area between the mean and z is 0.3413 (see Table 8.1). If we convert this area to a percentage (by multiplying by 100), then we see that 34.13% of cases fall between the z-score of 1.00 and a mean of 0.

Table 8.1. Excerpt from Table A.1 (z = 1.00)

Negative z-score

Positive z-score

Area between mean and z

Area beyond z

-1.00

1.00

0.3413

0.1587

From the table, you can also see that the area beyond z is 0.1587. Converting this to a percentage, we see that 15.87% of scores fall beyond a z-score of 1.00. The area beyond is also known as the tail area of the distribution.

Figure 8.6. Using a z-score to understand areas under the standard normal distribution.

Based on what we know about the normal distribution, we know that this shape is symmetrical (see Figure 8.6). So, the second and third column areas (red and blue areas in Figure 8.6) sum to 0.50 for their total area, meaning this area accounts for 50% of scores. Take any row in Table A.1, and the second and third columns will total 0.50.

Let’s look at a z-score of 1.00. We have two areas: the area between mean and z = 0.3413 and the area beyond z = 0.1587. If we add these two areas together, we get 0.3413 + 0.1587 = 0.50.

Table 8.2. Excerpt from Table A.1 (z = -1.00)

Negative z-score

Positive z-score

Area between mean and z

Area beyond z

-1.00

1.00

0.3413

0.1587

Also, because the distribution is symmetrical, you can use the information in Table A.1 for both positive and negative z-scores (see Table 8.2). For example, if you have a z-score of -1.00, you’d look up 1.00 and pull this same information about the red and blue areas. However, you would shade in these areas on the left-hand side of the distribution (because the negative scores are below the mean of 0 (see Figure 8.7). You’d still have an area between the mean and z of 0.3413, along with an area beyond z of 0.1587 (totaling 0.50). The only difference is that these areas are shaded on the left-hand, or negative side.

Figure 8.7. Example with z = −1, which has the same areas as z = 1, just on the negative side, illustrating the symmetrical nature of the distribution.

We often use z-score tables to help us answer questions about probability. For example, if you have a positive z-score, you may be interested in the probability of someone scoring higher than that positive score. To determine this, you would look up the area beyond z in the table.

In an earlier example, Sally scored z = 0.50 on their anxiety assessment. You are curious about the probability of someone scoring higher than Sally, so you look up z = 0.50 in Table A.1 and find that the area beyond z = 0.3085. Converting to a percentage, this means that there is a 30.85% probability of someone scoring higher than Sally (see Figure 8.8).

Figure 8.8. Sally’s anxiety assessment score and the probability of scoring higher than z = 0.50.

Sally also scored z = −0.50 on their depression assessment (so their score was on the negative side of the distribution). You could use this same information to see what the probability is of someone scoring lower than that negative score. So, using the area beyond z, there is also a 30.85% probability of someone scoring lower than Sally (see Figure 8.9).

Figure 8.9. Sally’s depression assessment score and the probability of scoring lower than z = −0.50.

 

If you had another client who scored z = −2.50, you could look up this z-score to find the area beyond z (which would be 0.0062). This means that there is a 0.62% probability that someone would score lower than this client. This information can be helpful if you need to compare this client to Sally (30.85% versus 0.62% probability).

Putting It All Together: Example With an Executive Functioning Assessment

Let’s work through one more example involving calculating z-scores, plotting them on the standard normal distribution, and using the z-score tables. For this example, you are a clinician who will assess clients’ executive functioning before starting an intervention for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). You use a standardized assessment, where scores range from 0 (low executive functioning problems) to 150 (high executive functioning problems), on a 1-point interval. Among children who seek services for ADHD interventions, the mean and standard deviation are μ = 92.5, σ = 15.5.

The scoring manual also specifies that children who score higher than 105 typically qualify for intervention. To get set up for screening participants, you want to answer the following: What is the probability that children will have a score greater than 105 (i.e., the probability of children qualifying for services)?

The first step is to calculate the z-score associated with a raw score of 105 (x = 105).

Example 8.4. Calculating z-Score for x = 105

Formula for z-score:

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example:

z = ( 105 − 92.5 ) 15.5 = 0.81

Next, you can look up the area beyond z in Table A.1 to determine the probability of children scoring greater than 105. The area beyond z for a z-score of 0.81 is 0.2090, or 20.90% (see Figure 8.10). Thus, there is a 20.90% probability that children will score higher than 105 and will be recommended for the intervention.

Figure 8.10. Standard normal distribution with z = 0.81 (with a 20.90% probability of scoring higher than z = 0.81).

As we continue into Chapter 9, we’ll see more examples of how we can use the z-score tables to help us answer questions about probability.

Summary

This chapter highlighted the utility of converting raw scores into z-scores, which utilizes the standard normal distribution. This distribution has a mean of 0 (at the center of the distribution), and a standard deviation of 1 (lines going above and below the mean at the center of the distribution are in increments of 1). If a z-score is positive, it is above the mean (of 0). If a z-score is negative, it is below the mean (of 0). Thus, you can transform any raw scores into z-scores and plot them on the standard normal distribution, and then you can easily make comparisons because they are on the same standard scale. We can use Table A.1 to further understand z-scores, examining the percentage of cases that fall in certain areas (between a z-score and the mean; the area beyond a z-score). This can be especially helpful if you have questions about the probability of scoring higher or lower than a positive or negative z-score, respectively.

9

Chapter 9: Percentile Scores and Cutoff Scores

In Chapter 8, we saw the utility of the standard normal distribution, calculating z-scores, and using a z-score table (Table A.1) to answer questions about probability. This chapter continues applications using z-scores: percentile scores and cutoff scores. Both can be used to further describe a single variable.

Percentile Scores

Another way in which z-scores can be helpful, especially when you want to make comparisons, is by calculating percentile scores. When we calculatepercentile scores, we find out the percentage of scores that fall below the observed score. We commonly see percentile scores used in standardized student tests (e.g., ACT or SAT); if you score in the 80th percentile, for example, then you scored higher in that domain than 80% of other people who took the test. Percentile scores are also helpful when tracking growth for children; if your child is in the 50th percentile for height, they are taller than 50% of other children that age.

Figure 9.1. “A Woman Writing on a Paper” by RDNE Stock project, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

To calculate a percentile score, you will first find the z-score and then use the z-table (Table A.1). The process is different depending on which side of the standard normal distribution you are on (positive versus negative):

  • If your z-score is negative, you are already on the left side of the distribution, so your percentile score is the area beyond z (or the tail region). This area tells you what percentage of people fall below that negative z-score.
  • If your z-score is positive, you are now on the right side of the distribution, which means you scored higher than those who would fall in the area between the mean and z, as well as the entire left side of the distribution (i.e., all the negative scores, so 0.50, or 50%). To find your percentile score, you’ll take the area between the mean and z + 0.50. This total area tells you the percentage of people who fall below that positive z-score.

Example: Percentile Scores for Assessment of Executive Functioning

In Chapter 8, our example used a standardized assessment of executive functioning, with μ = 92.5, σ = 15.5. Let’s find percentile scores for two clients who are screened for the attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) intervention:

  • Client A scores a 65 on the assessment. What is their percentile score?

Example 9.1. Calculating Percentile Score for Client A

Formula for z-score:

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example: 

z = ( 65 − 92.5 ) 15.5 = − 1.77

Because the z-score is negative (z = -1.77), the z-score for Client A will be on the left side of the distribution (1.77 standard deviations below the mean; see Figure 9.2). To find their percentile score, you would look up the z-score in Table A.1 and look up the area beyond z, which is 0.0384. Convert this to a percentage (3.84%). So, Client A scored higher on executive functioning than only 3.84% of all other clients.

Figure 9.2. Client A’s percentile score (they scored higher than 3.84% of others).
  • Client B scores 101 on the executive functioning assessment. What is their percentile score?

Example 9.2. Calculating Percentile Score for Client B

Formula for z-score:

z = ( x − μ ) σ

Our example: 

z = ( 101 − 92.5 ) 15.5 = 0.55

Because the z-score is positive (z = 0.55), the z-score will be on the right side of the distribution (0.55 standard deviations above the mean; see Figure 9.3). To find their percentile score, you would look up the z-score in Table A.1 and look up the area between the mean and z, which is 0.2088. You’ll then add 0.2088 to 0.50 (to account for all the negative z-scores that this client also scored higher than): 0.2088 + 0.50 = 0.7088. Convert this to a percentage (70.88%). So, Client B scored higher than 70.88% of clients.

Figure 9.3. Client B’s percentile score (they scored higher than 70.88% of others).

Percentile scores are another descriptive piece of information you can use to describe your client, participant, or patient. For another example, we will use the example from Chapter 8 where we saw that a z-score of 0.81 (raw score, x = 105) was a suggested score that would qualify clients with ADHD for intervention. First, we convert this to a percentile score, then look up z = 0.81 in Table A.1 and find the area between the mean and z = 0.2910. Next, we add 0.50: 0.2910 + 0.50 = 0.791. Your client would need to have a percentile score of 79.1% to “qualify for services” according to the test manual.

However, these are recommended scores based on research with norm samples. Drawing these lines can be difficult, especially if you have clients who have a percentile score of 78% – they may have high levels of executive functioning problems but they are 1% shy of “qualifying for services” according to this assessment. Thus, assessments can be seen as a guide, with further discussion being necessary if scores fall on these thresholds.

Cutoff Scores

Another application of z-scores is calculatingcutoff scores. These scores are useful when we are interested in a top percentage (e.g., the top 5% of scores are accepted into a group recovery program) or a bottom percentage (e.g., the bottom 10% of scores qualify for a remedial program). For cutoff scores, we will start with the percentage we are interested in and work backward to find the z-score and raw score (x) that are associated with the top or bottom percentage. You are solving for x, or the raw score that will serve as your cutoff score.

  • You will start by identifying the percentage or proportion of cases you are interested in working with.
  • Then, you will find the area beyond z in Table A.1 that is as close to that proportion as possible. For example, if you are interested in the top 10% of cases, you’ll find the area in the area beyond z column as close to 0.10 as possible. This is the row where the area beyond z = 0.1003 (10.03%).
  • Find the affiliated z-score in column 1. Note: If you are interested in the top percentage, you will use a positive z-score; if you are interested in the bottom percentage, you will make this affiliated z-score negative. So, if you are interested in the top 10%, your affiliated z-score would be 1.28; if you are interested in the bottom 10%, your affiliated z-score would be −1.28.
  • Finally, you will plug in this z-score to solve for x (your cut-off-score):

Formula 9.1. Calculating cutoff score

Formula for cutoff score (population):

x = z ( σ ) + μ

Formula for cutoff score (sample):

x = z ( s ) + x ¯

Example: Cutoff Scores for Top 10% and Bottom 15%

Your norm sample information is x̅ = 150, s = 10, and you want to find the cutoff score for the top 10%.

  • Identify the percentage you are interested in: top 10%.
  • Find the area beyond z that is as close to 10% as possible: area beyond z = 0.1003.
  • Affiliated z-score: Because you are interested in the top percentage, you will find the corresponding positive z-score: z = 1.28.
  • Plug these values into the equation to solve for x.

Example 9.3. Calculating Cutoff Score (Top 10%)

Formula for cutoff score:

x = z ( s ) + x ¯

Our example:

x = 1.28 ( 10 ) + 150

x = 12.8 + 150 = 162.8

So, your cutoff score = 162.8. This means an individual would have to score 162.8 or higher to be in the top 10%.

Let’s try this again, but now let’s say we are interested in the bottom 15%.

  • Identify the percentage you are interested in: bottom 15%.
  • Find the area beyond z that is as close to 15% as possible: area beyond z = 0.1492.
  • Affiliated z-score: Because you are interested in the bottom percentage, you will find the corresponding negative z-score: z = −1.04.
  • Plug these values into the equation to solve for x.

Example 9.4. Calculating Cut-off Score (Bottom 10%)

Formula for cutoff score:

x = z ( s ) + x ¯

Our example:

x = − 1.04 ( 10 ) + 150

x = − 10.4 + 150 = 139.6

So, your cutoff score = 139.6. This means an individual would have to score 139.6 or lower to be in the bottom 15%.

Common Cutoff Score Information

Table 9.1 shows some of the common top or bottom percentages that may be used for calculating cutoff scores, allowing you to find the area beyond z that is closest to the percentage you are interested in. However, 5% is a unique case, where there are two affiliated z-scores that are equidistant from 5%. You can choose a z-score of 1.64 (5.05%) or 1.65 (4.95%), or you can take the number between them (z = 1.645 or −1.645) if you want to get to exactly 5%.

Table 9.1. Common Cutoff Score Information
Top or bottom Area beyond z Area to % z-score value (top) z-score value (bottom)
5% .0505 5.05% 1.64 −1.64
.0495 4.95% 1.65 −1.65
– – (1.645) (−1.645)
10% .1003 10.03% 1.28 −1.28
15% .1492 14.92% 1.04 −1.04
20% .2005 20.05% 0.84 −0.84
25% .2514 25.14% 0.67 −0.67

As with the ethical implications of percentile scores, the same applies to cutoff scores. You can use cutoff scores to help guide decisions, but further discussion is warranted if a client falls right below or above a specified cutoff score.

Summary

This chapter highlighted two additional applications using z-scores: percentile scores and cutoff scores. Both can be used to further describe a single variable. Percentile scores can be useful when describing the percentage of scores that fall below the observed score. Cut-off scores are useful when you are interested in a top percentage (e.g., top 5%) or bottom percentage (e.g., bottom 20%) of scores. With cutoff scores, we start with the percentage we are interested in and work backward to find the z-score and raw score (x) that are associated with the top or bottom percentage.

IV

Unit 4. Introduction to Inferential Statistics and Hypothesis Testing

Up to this point in the book, we have focused on describing a sample or population. With continuous variables, we have been able to describe a variable in terms of its central tendency (mode, median, and mean) and variability (range, sum of squares, variance, standard deviation), plot this information on a normal distribution, assess the shape of our distribution, and standardize variables so that we can use the standard normal distribution for comparisons and answering questions about probability.

When using the normal distribution and standard normal distribution, we focused on comparing a single score (x) to a norm sample or a population. We calculated a z-score for a participant and used that information to make comparisons (e.g., assess probability and percentile scores). As we move into the second half of this book, we will now be focusing on samples, seeing how group scores relate to the population from which they came.

10

Chapter 10: Introduction to Inferential Statistics

Inferential statistics allow us to draw conclusions about populations based on randomly selected samples (i.e., sampled by methods of chance, such as drawing names from a hat) from these populations. So, our focus is now on samples; in social work, this could be groups of clients or patients, groups of participants in a program or intervention, groups of students, groups of families, community samples, and so forth. We want to see how these groups relate to the population from which they come. As we discussed in Chapter 2, it is not always feasible to hear from every single person that makes up a population (e.g., every member of a community), so we must rely on samples (e.g., a sample of 100 community members) and make inferences about the larger population.

For example, we may be interested in researching outcomes among people who have a substance use disorder (SUD) and are participating in motivational interviewing (for more information on motivational interviewing, see Smith [2024]). Our population would be all people who meet these criteria, but it would be impossible to survey or interview every single person who meets these criteria. So, we could take a sample of 100 clients who have a SUD and are participating in motivational interviewing. Then, we could calculate inferential statistics to make inferences about the population from which this sample of participants comes (see Figure 10.1).

 

Figure 10.1. Example showing how a sample is drawn from a population and inferences are made about that population.

Central Limit Theorem

Anytime we take a sample from a population, there is a chance we will have sampling error, or a difference between our sample statistic and the population parameter. We can assess and quantify the amount of sampling error by calculating the standard error and estimate how well we represented the population when we took a sample. We can quantify this amount of error using the central limit theorem. In most cases, we do not know what our population parameter is that we are trying to represent, so we rely on the central limit theorem to help us estimate the amount of expected sampling error (known as the standard error).

The first core tenet of the central limit theorem is that as your sample size increases, your sampling distribution of the sample statistic will approximate a normal distribution. A sampling distribution (of a statistic) is a theoretical distribution that results from taking an infinite number of random samples of the same size from the same population. This distribution is theoretical, but the tenets of the sampling distribution are used in all inferential statistics. Thus, we rely on the central limit theorem and its applications anytime we test an inferential hypothesis.

There are software programs that show simulations of the Central Limit Theorem, as well as other simulation tools used in math courses (e.g.,Hagtvedt et al., 2007; Ruggieri, 2016). Simulations have you start with a population distribution–it can be any shape (e.g., normal or non-normal shape, such as a uniform distribution or a heavily skewed distribution). Then, the simulation pulls repeated samples of the same size. For each of these samples, the mean is calculated. Then, you plot all the means from each of these samples. Once you plot all the means, your distribution will approximate the normal distribution. This is the power of the central limit theorem: Even if our population data are not normally distributed, you can rely on the sampling distribution (which approximates the normal distribution) to test your inferential research question. This is ideal; see Chapter 7 on the utility of the normal distribution.

From these simulations, the three principles of the Central Limit Theorem are illustrated. In this chapter and the next few chapters, we’ll be examining inferential tests that use sampling distributions of sample means (x̅) as a foundation.

The central limit theorem tenets pertain to the following:

  • Shape: As the sample size increases, the shape of the sampling distribution of x̅ approximates normality (approximates the normal distribution), which allows us to use statistical analyses based on the normal distribution.
  • Mean: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the mean in the population from which samples were randomly selected.
  • Variability: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution decreases as the sample size increases; in other words, larger samples lead to more accurate estimates (with less sampling error). We can compute this expected sampling error (also known as the standard error) using the equation for calculating the standard error.

Formula 10.1. Formula for standard error

σ x ¯ = σ N

A few additional notes about these components of the central limit theorem are warranted. As a reminder, theorems are mathematical statements that have been proven to be true.

First, even if the population distribution is heavily skewed, platykurtic or leptokurtic, uniform, or any non-normal shape, but you take many large random sample means from the population, the shape of your sampling distribution of means will still approximate a normal distribution. This will allow you to run inferential statistical tests using what we know about a normal distribution.

Second, much of the central limit theorem revolves around the idea of sample size. Recommendations across texts range from minimum sample sizes of N > 30 to as high as N > 200 (e.g., Magsalay, 2025) for your sampling distribution shape to approximate a normal distribution. If the population distribution is strongly non-normal (e.g., heavily skewed), the larger sample size recommendations may be needed (Islam, 2018). Taking a more conservative approach, it is recommended to have sample sizes of N > 200 for more reliable approximations.

Simulation of Creating a Sampling Distribution of Means

Let’s simulate our own sampling distribution of means. According to the U.S. Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention (OJJDP; Puzzanchera et al., 2025), in 2023, the average age of youth detained for juvenile offenses was 16 (N = 29,314). The distribution of ages is negatively skewed; most youth who were detained for a juvenile offense were between the ages of 16 and 17. Only a few youth who were detained were 13 or younger (see Figure 10.2).

Figure 10.2. Example skewed population distribution.

If we wanted to ask a research question concerning this population, we would likely have to rely on a sample; it would be difficult to obtain surveys or interviews from all 29,314 youth. This is where we can rely on inferential statistics to help us sample this population. We hope to represent this population well, and minimize the amount of expected sampling error.

For our simulation, we are going to take 30 samples from this population; each sample will be 200 people. Note: In computer software simulations of creating sampling distributions, programs take very large numbers of samples (i.e., get close to infinity). This example of 30 is nowhere near these simulations, but because of space constraints, we will use it for illustrative purposes.

Across our 30 samples of 200 people each, we have the following sample means.
