Although this simulation is only with 30 sample means, you can still see the components of the theorem in action. You could re-calculate the standard error with N = 2,000 and see how this reduces the standard error estimate to 0.03. This illustrates that if our random samples to make a sampling distribution are larger, we can reduce the amount of expected sampling error.

Summary

Thanks to the central limit theorem, we know something about the shape, central tendency, and variability of the theoretical sampling distribution, which we can then use within inferential tests. We can take a single sample and compare it with the sampling distribution and assess the probability that our sample came from the same population.

11

Chapter 11: Confidence Intervals

In the world of inferential statistics, we are taking a sample and making inferences about the population it came from. As we read in Chapter 10, the central limit theorem provides us with a way to make inferences about a population based on a sample. We can estimate the amount of expected sampling error when we conduct inferential statistics. This chapter introduces confidence intervals, a way for us to further assess the inferences we are making.

Confidence Intervals

Confidence intervals provide us with a way to assess our level of confidence in representing the population; they can tell us with 95% or 99% confidence that we have represented the population with our sample statistic. Thus, confidence intervals give us a range within which the population parameter is located.

  • 95% Confidence Interval: the range within which a population parameter is located, with 95% confidence.
  • 99% Confidence Interval: the range within which a population parameter is located, with 99% confidence.

If we think about the key features of the normal distribution, approximately 95% of scores are located within 2 standard deviations of the mean, and approximately 99% of scores are located within 3 standard deviations of the mean. So, we’ll use Table A.1 to help us find the exact standard deviations from the mean (i.e., z-scores) that give us 95% and 99% confidence.

With both 95% and 99% confidence intervals, there is a 5% and 1% (respectively) chance that we did not include the population parameter in our confidence interval range. Because we are using samples to make inferences, we will always have a chance for error or not representing the mean.

For example, let’s pretend we know our population mean is 50. This population mean is outlined in red at the center of the distribution in Figure 11.1; this is what we are trying to represent when we take samples. If we took three samples and calculated their means and confidence intervals, they would be plotted as shown in Figure 11.1. The mean for each sample is outlined in red, with the confidence interval brackets extending lower and higher around the mean. We would expect the population parameter to fall somewhere in that bracketed area. If it falls outside of the confidence interval, then we did not represent the population mean.

Let’s look at each sample:

Figure 11.1. Samples A-C and their confidence intervals.
  • Sample A: The mean is at the center of the line (x̅ is 48), and the confidence interval gives a value below the mean and above the mean. So, from the lower value to the upper value of the confidence interval bracket, we have 95% confidence that we represented the population mean. In this example, the population mean is inside the bracketed area, so Sample A included the population parameter it was trying to represent.
  • Sample B: The sample mean (x̅ is 28) and the confidence interval bracket do not include the population mean. This would be an example of the 5% of the time when your sample does not represent the population parameters.
  • Sample C: The sample mean (x̅ is 69) and the confidence interval bracket do include the population, although it is very close.

In most situations, we will not know the population parameter we are trying to represent, so we can rely on confidence intervals to say with either 95% or 99% confidence that we represented the parameter.

Calculating 95% Confidence Intervals

To find the lower and upper values of our confidence intervals, we’ll use Table A.1 to find the exact proportion we are interested in (95%). If you look up z = 1.96 in the z-score table (Table A.1), you’ll see that the area between the mean and z = 0.475. Because your distribution is symmetrical, you have 0.475 between 1.96 and a mean of 0, and you have 0.475 between −1.96 and a mean of 0. So, together, these areas equal 0.95, which converts to a percentage of 95%. Thus, 95% of cases are located within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean.

So, when we are extending the confidence interval bracket above and below the sample mean, we can extend that 1.96 standard deviations in both directions from the sample mean. We can be 95% confident that we include the population in that confidence interval. See Figure 11.2.

Figure 11.2. Distribution showing 95% confidence intervals (area between z = −1.96 and 1.96 totals 0.95, or 95%).

 

To calculate the 95% confidence interval of your population mean (again, this is what you are hoping to include when you take your sample), you will need to calculate the standard error. Note: Because we are calculating the standard error based on the central limit theorem, we will also want to make sure we have a sample size of 200 or more. This will ensure that we are approximating a normal distribution.

Formula 11.1. Calculating 95% confidence intervals

Formula for 95% confidence interval of population mean:
μ = x ¯ ± ( 1.96 × s x ¯ )
Steps for calculating 95% confidence interval of population mean: 
  1. Calculate the standard error using ( s x ¯ = s N ) .
  2. Multiply the standard error by 1.96. Remember, 1.96 is the z-score that will give you the proportion you are interested in: 95%.
  3. Take the product (from step 2) and add it to the sample mean. This value becomes the upper part of your bracket or confidence interval value, above the sample mean.
  4. Take the product (from step 2) and subtract it from the sample mean. This value becomes the lower part of your bracket or confidence interval value, below the sample mean.

Example: 95% Confidence Interval for Estimating the Monthly Benefit of SNAP

According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (2025), individuals enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), received an average monthly benefit of $177 (based on an average household size of 1.9 people). You collect a sample of individuals (N = 425) in your service area who are receiving SNAP benefits. For your sample, your x̅ = 180, and the standard deviation is 42. In this case, you know the average you hope to represent ($177), although in many instances, you will not know this population information. Let’s calculate a 95% confidence interval.

Example 11.1. Calculating 95% Confidence Interval

Formula for 95% Confidence Interval of Population Mean:
μ = x ¯ ± ( 1.96 × s x ¯ )
Steps for Calculating 95% Confidence Interval of Population Mean in our example: 
  1. Calculate the standard error:  s x ¯ = s N s x ¯ = 42 425 = 2.04 .
  2. Multiply the standard error by 1.96: 1.96 × 2.04 = 4.00 .
  3. Take the product (from step 2) and add it to the sample mean 180 + 4 = 184.
  4. Take the product (from step 2) and subtract it from the sample mean 180 − 4 = 176.

So, your 95% confidence interval (CI) of 𝜇 is 176 and 184. You may see this notated in texts as 95% CI = [176, 184]. These values give you the lower and upper boundaries of a range where you have 95% confidence that you represented the population mean. In this example, our population mean was 177, so it is within this confidence interval.

Calculating 99% Confidence Intervals

To find the lower and upper values of our confidence intervals, we’ll use Table A.1 to find the exact proportion we are interested in (99%). If you look up z = 2.58 in the z-score table (Table A.1.), you’ll see that the area between the mean and z = 0.495. Because the distribution is symmetrical, we have 0.495 between 2.58 and a mean of 0, and we have 0.495 between −2.58 and a mean of 0. So, together, these areas equal 0.99, which converts to a percentage of 99%. Thus, 99% of cases are located within 2.58 standard deviations of the mean. So, when we are extending the confidence interval bracket above and below the sample mean, we can extend the 2.58 standard deviation in both directions from the sample mean. We can be 95% confident that we included the population in that confidence interval. See Figure 11.3.

Figure 11.3. Distribution with 99% confidence intervals (area between z = −2.58 and 2.58 totals 0.99, or 99%).

 

To calculate the 99% confidence interval of your population mean, you will need to calculate the standard error. Note: Because we are calculating the standard error based on the central limit theorem, we will also want to make sure we have a sample size of 200 or more. This will ensure that we are approximating a normal distribution.

Formula 11.2: Calculating 99% confidence intervals

Formula for 99% confidence interval of population mean:
μ = x ¯ ± ( 2.58 × s x ¯ )
Steps for calculating 99% confidence interval of population mean: 
  1. Calculate the standard error using ( s x ¯ = s N ) .
  2. Multiply the standard error by 2.58. Remember, 2.58 is the z-score that will give you the proportion you are interested in: 99%.
  3. Take the product (from step 2) and add it to the sample mean. This value becomes the upper part of your bracket or confidence interval value above the sample mean.
  4. Take the product (from step 2) and subtract it from the sample mean. This value becomes the lower part of your bracket or confidence interval value below the sample mean.

Example: 99% Confidence Intervals for Estimating the Monthly Benefit of SNAP

Let’s try our previous example, but this time let’s calculate a 99% confidence interval. As a reminder, here’s the sample information: N = 425,

x̅ = 180, and standard deviation = 42.

Example 11.2. Calculating 99% Confidence Interval

Formula for 99% Confidence Interval of Population Mean:
μ = x ¯ ± ( 2.58 × s x ¯ )
Steps for Calculating 99% Confidence Interval of Population Mean in our example: 
  1. Calculate the standard error:  s x ¯ = s N s x ¯ = 42 425 = 2.04 .
  2. Multiply the standard error by 2.58 2.58 × 2.04 = 5.26 .
  3. Take the product (from step 2) and add it to the sample mean. 180 + 5.26 = 185.26 .
  4. Take the product (from step 2) and subtract it from the sample mean. 180 − 5.26 = 174.74 .

So, your 95% Confidence Interval (CI) of 𝜇 is 174.74 and 185.26. You may see this notated in texts as 99% CI = [174.74, 185.26]. These values give you the lower and upper boundaries of a range where you have 99% confidence that you represented the population mean. In this example, our population mean was 177, so it is within this confidence interval.

Confidence intervals of 99% include a larger area of the normal distribution (between 2.58 standard deviations of the mean), so this widens the range. So, you’re expanding the range, and you are now 99% confident.  Confidence intervals of 95% have a narrower range; you are only 95% confident.

Summary

In the world of inferential statistics, we can never be 100% confident in our estimates. However, we can calculate confidence intervals with 95% or 99% confidence that we represented our population parameter. As we continue into Chapter 12, we will continue to see these areas of confidence and the ways in which we use them in inferential statistics.

12

Chapter 12: Hypothesis Testing (with the z-test)

Chapters 10 and 11 oriented you to the central limit theorem, which provide you with estimates pertaining to the expected sampling error (i.e., standard error) and confidence intervals. This chapter will continue to introduce you to topics within the world of inferential statistics, including hypothesis testing, which is a step-by-step process in testing your research hypothesis with an inferential statistics test. A hypothesis is an informed assumption or prediction about your research question. Hypothesis testing will introduce new language and phrases that are used throughout the steps.

Hypothesis Testing and Probability

The basis of all inferential statistics tests is grounded in probability, which assesses how likely or probable it is that a result you obtain occurred by random chance. For example, there is a .50 or 50% probability that you will flip a coin and end up with heads. You may have probabilities that range from 0 (i.e., zero probability of something happening) to 1.00 or 100% (i.e., absolute probability of something happening). Remember that in inferential statistics, we are using a sample to make inferences or conclusions about the population it comes from. So, we can never be 100% certain that we have a sample that reflects the population (although, as we saw in Chapter 11, we can have 95% and 99% confidence).

As we calculate inferential statistics results, we can quantify the probability of our result being due to chance or due to a meaningful difference from our sample. For example, if you take a sample from a population, you may want to test to see whether that sample is different from the population (i.e., there’s something unique about your sample) or is a representation of that population (i.e., your sample reflects the population from which it came).

Example: Assessing Need for Trauma-Informed Therapies Using Hypothesis Testing

Let’s say you are working with a group of women who are incarcerated and are trying to assess the need for trauma-informed therapies (e.g., Trauma-Focused Cognitive Behavioral Therapy or Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing; Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration [SAMHSA], 2014; Yadav et al., 2024) at the facility where you work. You have a random sample of women (N = 300) complete a questionnaire about their adverse childhood experiences (ACEs; Felitti et al., 1998). You also review their case records to assess their number of prior incarcerations.

You may have a research question that you want to test, which involves comparing your sample to the population (i.e., all women who are incarcerated in the U.S.) mean.

  • Research Question: Does this sample of women have significantly different levels of prior incarcerations compared to all women who are incarcerated?
  • If you find that your sample does have significantly different levels (we will walk through the steps of determining this), then your sample has significantly different levels of prior incarcerations than the whole population.
  • If you find that your sample does not have significantly different levels, then your sample is like the population.

Our hypotheses are guided by our research questions; sometimes we hypothesize that our sample is different from the population or unique. For example, maybe our sample includes women with higher security levels with more violent histories, so we would hypothesize that our sample would have a different (i.e., higher) average level of prior incarcerations than all women who are incarcerated.

Figure 12.1. “Person in Black Pants Standing on Gray Carpet” by Tima Miroshnichenko, via Pexels, 2020. Pexels license.

Testing these inferential statistics questions with hypothesis testing will involve probability. We have already seen probability when we looked at the normal distribution. For example, we could ask about the probability of selecting a z-score of 1.5 standard deviations above the mean (see Chapter 7). We would look up the area beyond z in Table A.1 to find the probability of finding a score in this region. For example, with a z-score of 1.5, the proportion of cases beyond z is 0.0668; thus, there is a 6.68% chance of a z-score being higher than 1.5. If we have a z-score of 3, this area is 0.0013, and we have a 0.13% chance of a z-score being higher than 3.

We’ll use probability to guide hypothesis testing as well. If we see a low probability, this means that there is a low probability that this statistic represents the population; in other words, this sample is significantly different from the population.

When describing probability in hypothesis testing, we’ll use the following guidelines:

  • Low probability (i.e., small p value or probability value) that a sample comes from a population: significant difference.
  • High probability (i.e., larger p value) that a sample comes from a population: not a significant difference.

As we continue in this chapter, we’ll define what constitutes a “small p value” and what makes something “significant” or “not significant.”

The Logic of the Hypothesis Test

As an inferential statistical procedure, hypothesis testing includes four steps. As you collect quantitative data from your sample, you will write a hypothesis about the population from which you pulled the sample. So, Steps 1 and 4 will refer to that population about which you are making inferences.

  1. Hypothesis Pair
    • Null hypothesis, Ho: Statement of no difference
    • Alternative hypothesis, Ha: Statement of difference

  2. Setup for the Test

    • What inferential test are you using?
    • Set your confidence/alpha.
    • Find your critical value(s).

  3. Test Statistic computation

    • Solve for your obtained value.

  4. Make a decision

    • Reject the null hypothesis.
    • Fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

First, you are going to write up your hypothesis pair to articulate what you are testing. You’ll have a null hypothesis and an alternative hypothesis.

  • The null hypothesis, notated as Ho is your statement of no difference. This is when you obtain a sample statistic and expect it to be like your population parameter. For example, you’d expect your sample mean to fall between 1.96 standard deviations of your population mean, with 95% confidence.
  • The alternative hypothesis, notated as Ha is your statement of difference. This is often your research hypothesis. For example, if you expect your sample statistic to be different from your population (e.g., statistic falls beyond the confidence interval of the population mean), this would be the statement to hypothesize that difference. You may hypothesize that your sample would have a higher value, a lower value, or be different (i.e., higher or lower) from the population parameter. You will specify this in your hypothesis pair write-up. For this chapter, we will walk through a hypothesis where you want to see if your sample is different from than the population; Chapter 13 will walk you through an example of when you specifically hypothesize higher or lower values.

This pair of statements is always written together, and the alternative hypothesis always negates the null hypothesis; so, if one hypothesis statement is true, the other is false.

For this step and the rest of our steps, we’ll continue the same example as detailed earlier: According to the 2016 Profile of Prison Inmates (U.S. Department of Justice, 2021), females who were incarcerated at the time of the survey had an average of five prior incarcerations in their lifetime. We sample a group of female participants (N = 300) who are incarcerated in Illinois and calculate their average number of prior incarcerations. We want to know if there is a significant difference between our sample mean and the federal population mean.

In this chapter, we will compare one sample mean to a population mean and standard deviation (often provided to you through an assessment manual that provides information about a normed sample, or a large, representative group that was used to develop the norms for the population). We will be testing this comparison with the z-test. The z-test allows you to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (𝜇).

For this example, our research question is as follows: Do females incarcerated in Illinois have different levels of prior incarcerations compared with the national average?

Federal population: 𝜇 = 5, σ = 1.6.

Your sample: x̅ = 4.8, s = 1.9, N = 300.

First, we’ll write our hypothesis pair for step 1 of our hypothesis test:

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 = 5.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 ≠ 5.

This can also be notated like this:

  • Ho: μ1 = 5.
  • Ha: μ1 ≠ 5.

We are referring to our population mean in these statements. Table 12.1 shows a break down of all the elements.

Table 12.1. Elements of the Hypothesis Pair Statements

Element

Description of the Hypothesis Pair Statement Elements

Ho

Notation for null hypothesis

Ha

Notation for alternative hypothesis

μ1

Mu (population mean): because we are testing an inferential test, we are making hypotheses and inferences about a population. There is a subscript “1”–this is because we are taking one sample and comparing its mean to the population mean.

= or ≠

We will be testing to see if there is a difference (≠) or no difference (=).

5

In our example, our population mean is 5. So, we are including this in our hypothesis pair statement to see if we can infer that our sample is or is not significantly different from 5.

As you’ll see in Chapter 13, you can also have a directional alternative hypothesis. This means that you hypothesize that your sample will have either higher levels than the population (>) or lower levels than the population (<). So, your alternative hypothesis would use “>” or “<” instead of “≠” in the statement. However, for the rest of this chapter, we will focus on differences and use “≠” in our alternative hypothesis statement.

Step 2: Set-up for the Test

This step is all about setting up information for testing your hypotheses. There are three elements to this step: (1) determining what inferential test you will use, (2) setting your confidence and alpha levels, and (3) finding your critical value or values.

First, you will determine your inferential test. In Chapters 12 and 13, we will be using the z-test. Again, the z-test allows you to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (𝜇). As you’ll see in later chapters, you will be looking at hypothesis tests for other types of inferential tests. We will note the implications those inferential test selections will have on the rest of the hypothesis test in those specific chapters.

Second, you will set your confidence and alpha levels. This is also called setting your significance level. These numbers provide you with the threshold for making decisions about your hypotheses.

  • Confidence: This is the total area of the distribution that is not in the tail or tails of a distribution. Commonly, you’ll see people set their confidence level at 95%, but you can also set it to 99% or another confidence level. For the rest of this book, we will examine hypothesis testing with 95% confidence.
  • Alpha (α): This is the total area of the distribution that is in the tail or tails of a distribution. Because the alpha and confidence areas add up to 1.00, or 100%, your alpha area would be set at 0.05, or 5% if your confidence is set to 0.95, or 95%.

In this chapter, we will be testing whether our sample is “different” from a population (i.e., could be lower or higher), so we will be testing both tails (i.e., tail on each side of the distribution). Because we are testing both tails, we are going to split our alpha area of 0.05, or 5% into the left side (0.025, or 2.5%) and right side (0.025, or 2.5%). Then, our confidence is everything in between, totaling .95, or 95%. Confidence can be defined as 1 – α, so in this example, 1 – .05 = 0.95.

Third, you find your critical value or values. Because we will be testing two tails (remember, we split the alpha), you will have two critical values. Critical values are the values that divide your alpha and confidence areas. Because we are calculating a z-test, we can use our z-score table (Table A.1) to find our critical values.

Earlier, we set our confidence level to 95%. So, that leaves 5% total alpha. The z-scores that gives us 95% confidence are 1.96 and -1.96. If we look up the area beyond z for these z-scores, it is 0.025. We have two tails, so 0.025 × 2 = 0.05. This totals our .05, or 5% alpha area. So, that means our critical values are 1.96 and −1.96. These are notated in Figure 12.2 as “zc” for “z-critical.”

Figure 12.2. Set-up for a z-test; your z-critical values (−1.96 and 1.96) separate your alpha (tail regions) from your confidence area (under the high point of the curve). Together, your alpha and confidence areas total 1.00, or 100%.

 

As shown in the figure, your confidence area is set to 95% and includes the area between z = −1.96 and 1.96. The alpha area is split between your two tails and is the area beyond the z-scores of −1.96 and 1.96. Your total alpha area is 5%, and it is split between two tails, so 2.5% in each tail. You will use this image to guide the rest of your hypothesis test. Note: If we wanted to set our confidence to 99%, z-scores of −2.58 and 2.58 would be our critical values.

To summarize Step 2, we do the following:

  • Determine what inferential test you are using: We will use the z-test because we want to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (𝜇).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95 (95%), and alpha = .05 (5% total split between two tails).
  • Find your critical value(s): zc = ±1.96.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

In this step, you will compute your test statistic, or your “obtained value,” using the inferential test you selected in Step 2. As a reminder, your federal population mean is 𝜇 = 5, and the standard deviation is 𝜎 = 1.6. Your sample mean (N = 300) is x̅ = 4.8. We will be using the z-test to compare our sample mean of 4.8 to the population mean of 5 and see if they are significantly different.

Because we are using a sample to make inferences, we will first calculate the standard error (i.e., expected sampling error). Then, we can use this standard error and solve for the z-obtained value.

Formula 12.1. Calculating standard error and z-obtained

Formula for standard error: 

σ x ¯ = σ N

Formula for z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( x ¯ − μ ) σ x ¯

Example 12.1. Finding Standard Error and z-obtained Values

Formula for standard error: 

σ x ¯ = σ N

Formula for z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( x ¯ − μ ) σ x ¯

Our example standard error: 

σ x ¯ = 1.6 300 = 0.09

Our example z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( 4.8 − 5 ) 0.09 = − 2.22

For our example, our z-obtained value is −2.22.

Step 4: Make a Decision

Finally, in Step 4, you’ll make an inference based on your previous steps. The language used in Step 4 includes selecting one of two phrases:

“Reject the null hypothesis” or “Fail to reject the null hypothesis.”

If you remember back to Step 1, the null hypothesis is the statement of no difference; the sample mean and population mean are not significantly different. So, our statement selection is based on the logic of falsification. We will use our distribution visual to help us with our decision. We will see where our obtained value (found in Step 3) falls in relation to your confidence and alpha areas.

  • If the obtained value falls in the confidence area: You would “fail to reject the null hypothesis” because your obtained value from your sample falls in the area in which you are 95% confident that the population mean is represented. This would mean that there is not a significant difference between your sample mean and the population mean. You would infer that there not is a significant difference.
  • If the obtained value falls in the alpha area: You would “reject the null hypothesis,” because your obtained value from your sample falls beyond the area (as defined by your critical values) in which you are 95% confident that the population mean is represented. This would mean that there is a significant difference between your sample mean and the population mean. You would infer that there is a significant difference.

Let’s look at our example. Our z-obtained value is −2.22. If we plot this on our distribution (which has our confidence and alpha areas labeled from Step 2), as shown in Figure 12.3, we see that our obtained value falls in the alpha area on the negative side of our distribution. So, we would reject the null hypothesis. In other words, our sample has significantly different levels of prior incarcerations than the federal average.

Figure 12.3. Plotting our z-obtained value on our distribution (which we set up in step 2 of the hypothesis test).

Making an Inference Based on the Hypothesis Test: APA-Style Write-up

After you go through the four steps, you will make an inference about your findings. Typically, reports suggest including components outlined by the American Psychological Association (APA, 2020). You’ll want to introduce the type of test you conducted, report key values (e.g., means and obtained value), and indicate whether you found a significant difference or not. For our example, we could write the following in a report:

A one-sample z-test was calculated to compare the average number of prior incarcerations from a sample of women who are currently incarcerated in Illinois to the mean found with a large, federal survey. Based on a sample size of 300, women in Illinois who were incarcerated had a significantly different average of prior incarcerations (mean [M] = 4.8, standard deviation [SD] = 1.9) than the national average (M = 5), z = −2.22, p < .05.

This type of result may lead you to test other hypotheses to try to understand why this sample is significantly different from the national average. Some of the key components of the APA-style write-up include the following:

  • Use of “M” for means; rather than using symbol notation for population and sample means, APA style typically uses “M” when writing up the results for means. You can also include your sample standard deviation (termed “SD” in these write-ups). This standard deviation for the sample is not used in any of the calculations; it is just listed here in case readers are interested in sample-specific descriptive statistics. Although the population standard deviation is used in analyses, they are typically not presented in the APA-style write-up.
  • The notation of “z = −2.22”: This is your obtained value from Step 3 of the hypothesis test.
  • “Significantly different” means you rejected the null hypothesis in Step 4 of the hypothesis test.
  • The notation of “p < .05”: This also indicates to readers that you rejected the null hypothesis. This means that there is a less than (<) 5% probability (p) that this sample represents the population; there is something significantly different about this sample of women. Again, if you have a small probability (defined here as less than 5%, which was set in Step 2 of the hypothesis test), then there is a small probability that your sample represents the population; there is something different about your sample. Because you set these confidence and alpha areas in Step 2, the difference is large enough that it is unlikely to be due to chance.

Probability values (p Values)

Probability values, or p values, are computed alphas.

  • When the p value is less than your set alpha (e.g., 0.05), you reject the null hypothesis.
  • When the p value is greater than your set alpha (e.g., 0.05), you fail to reject the null hypothesis.

You can use “p < .05” to indicate your set threshold and where your obtained value fell (in the alpha area), or you can find the exact p value or probability. Look up your z-obtained value in the z-table (Table A.1), and look up the area beyond z. Then, because you tested both tails, you will take that area and multiply it by 2. This will give you your exact p value or probability.

In our example, our z = −2.22. Our area beyond z = 0.0132. We tested for a difference in either tail area, so we will multiply our probability by 2. So, 0.0132 × 2 = 0.0264. This means there is a 2.64% probability that your sample came from your population. Because this is less than 5% (your set significance level from Step 2), you would say this is a significant difference. Therefore, your p value statement about significance can be written as follows: “p < .05” or “p = .0264.” Both statements indicate a significant difference. Here’s the APA-style write-up again with the exact p value:

A one-sample z-test was calculated to compare the average number of prior incarcerations from a sample of women who are currently incarcerated in Illinois to the mean found with a large, federal survey. Based on a sample size of 300, women in Illinois who were incarcerated had a significantly different average of prior incarcerations (M = 4.8, SD = 1.9) than the national average (M = 5), z = −2.22, p = .0264.

If you think back to earlier in this chapter, we saw that together, the alpha and confidence areas total 1.00, or 100%. So, if we know our exact p value (alpha area), then we can take 1 – (alpha area) to find our maximum confidence. In our example, alpha = 0.0264, so confidence = 1 – 0.0264 = 0.9736, or 97.36%. This value of 97.36% also exceeds our significance level from Step 2, which said we needed at least 95% confidence. So, our maximum confidence also tells us that we have a significant difference.

Let’s try another hypothesis testing example using a z-test:

Example: Suicide Risk in a Co-Response Team Using Hypothesis Testing

As part of a co-response team, a social worker and a police officer respond to mental health-related dispatch calls. For more information on co-response models and other types of crisis intervention teams, see Eaton et al. (2025) and Watson et al. (2017). The social worker uses a standardized suicide risk assessment; if scores are near 50, then this indicates a low risk for suicide, scores between 60 and 70 indicate increasing risk of suicidal thoughts or behaviors, and scores 70 and above indicate a high risk of suicidal behaviors. The social worker wants to do hypothesis testing to see whether their sample of subjects from the past quarter had different levels of suicidal risk compared with the norm sample. The social worker calculates their sample mean and compares it to the norm sample mean and standard deviation. They will be using a z-test in a hypothesis testing framework.

Research question: Does this sample of subjects have different levels of suicide risk compared with the norm average?

Population mean and standard deviation: 𝜇 = 56, σ = 3.7.

Your sample: x̅ = 56.8, s = 3.4, N = 65.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

  • Null hypothesis: μ1= 56.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 ≠ 56.

This can also be notated as follows:

  • Ho: μ1= 56.
  • Ha: μ1 ≠ 56.

Step 2: Set-up for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? We will use the z-test (because we want to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (μ).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.
  • Find your critical value(s): zc = ±1.96.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

First, solve for the standard error, using the population standard deviation (3.7) divided by the square root of your sample size (65). Then, use that value to find your z-obtained value.

Population mean and standard deviation: 𝜇 = 56, σ = 3.7.

Your sample: x̅ = 56.8, s = 3.4, N = 65.

Example 12.2. Finding the Standard Error and z-Obtained Values

Formula for standard error: 

σ x ¯ = σ N

Formula for z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( x ¯ − μ ) σ x ¯

Our example standard error: 

σ x ¯ = 3.7 65 = 0.46

Our example z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( 56.8 − 56 ) 0.46 = 1.74

For our example, the z-obtained value is 1.74.

Step 4: Make a Decision

If we plot where our z-obtained value (z = 1.74) falls in relation to the confidence and alpha areas (as defined in Step 2), we see that our obtained value falls in the confidence area of the distribution (see Figure 12.4).

Figure 12.4. Plotting our z-obtained value on our distribution (which we set-up in Step 2 of the hypothesis test).

This means that we will fail to reject the null hypothesis, which means that our sample is not significantly different from the norm sample mean. This sample of subjects has an average score that falls in the confidence area of the distribution, meaning that it falls in the area we would expect a sample pulled from the population to fall. So, we fail to be able to reject our null hypothesis (which states that our sample is no different from our population mean).

Let’s go ahead and find our exact p value and maximum confidence level, before writing up the results for our report. To find exact p value, we will look up our z-obtained value in Table A.1. The area beyond z = 0.0409. We tested both tails, so our total alpha area = .0409 × 2 = 0.0818. This is not less than (<) .05 (our set significance level), so we do not have a significant difference. For our maximum confidence, we will take 1 – alpha, so 1 – 0.0818, which equals 0.9182, or 91.82%. This is not greater than 95%, so again, we do not have a significant difference.

Figure 12.5. “Man and Policewoman Talking in the Street” by Kindel Media, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

APA Write-up

Our APA-style write-up would be as follows:

A one-sample z-test was calculated to compare the average suicidal risk assessment scores from a sample of dispatch call subjects with the norm average. Based on mental health-related calls from the previous quarter (N = 65), this sample did not have significantly different levels of suicidal risk (M = 56.8, SD = 3.4) than the norm average (M = 56), z = 1.74, p > .05.

The second sentence could also state the exact p value rather than “p > 0.05”:

Based on mental health-related calls from the previous quarter (N = 65), this sample did not have significantly different levels of suicidal risk (M = 56.8, SD = 3.4) than the norm average (M = 56), z = 1.74, p = .0818.

Summary

This chapter outlined the four steps of the hypothesis test framework while also introducing the language used throughout the steps. We reviewed the z-test using hypothesis testing and found a significant difference (“rejected the null hypothesis”) in the first example, but we didn’t find a significant difference (“failed to reject the null hypothesis”) in the second example. We reviewed the differences between these two outcomes in terms of language and p values. We concluded this chapter with APA-style statements about how to write about these findings in a report, including how to find and report p values and maximum confidence level.

13

Chapter 13: Additional Hypothesis Testing Considerations

In the previous chapter, we learned about the hypothesis testing framework, which includes the four steps for testing a research question using the z-test. This chapter continues to discuss hypothesis testing with the z-test, highlighting directional hypotheses, as well as errors and limitations that can occur when using an inferential test within the hypothesis testing framework.

Directional Hypothesis

In Chapter 12, we tested research questions where we split our alpha areas into two tails; in other words, we tested whether there was a difference, but we weren’t sure if our sample mean would be higher (positive z-score) or lower (negative z-score) than the population mean. By using a two-tailed test, this gives us two areas (2.5% in each tail) where we could potentially see a significant difference (see Figure 13.1).

Figure 13.1. Two-tailed test set-up.

A directional hypothesis test can also be written, which is also referred to as a one-tailed test. When you have a strong reason to believe that your sample mean will fall higher or lower in relation to your population mean, you can indicate this throughout your hypothesis test. This means you have just one alpha area, or one tail that you are testing.

As shown in Figure 13.2, you may hypothesize that your sample mean is higher than the population mean, in which case you would have just the alpha area on the positive side of the distribution (and as shown later, your z-critical would be 1.65). Or you may hypothesize that your sample mean is lower than the population mean, in which case you would have just the alpha area on the negative side of the distribution (z-critical = −1.65), as shown in Figure 13.3. In both figures, your alpha area is only on one side, so the total 5% is in that area (rather than split, as in a two-tailed test).

Figure 13.2. One-tailed test (positive).
Figure 13.3. One-tailed test (negative).

Next, we will see how directional hypotheses affect the hypothesis testing steps.

First, in Step 1, you will indicate a directional hypothesis with your alternative hypothesis statement. Rather than using “≠”, you will use “<” or “>,” depending on your hypothesis.

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 =____(value of your population mean)
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 >_____ (value of your population mean)

or

  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 <_____ (value of your population mean)

Example: Prior Incarcerations with a Directional Hypothesis

Let’s use our example from Chapter 12, where your research question was as follows: Do females incarcerated in Illinois have different levels of prior incarcerations compared with the national average? Recall that the federal population mean is 𝜇 = 5 and the standard deviation is 𝜎 = 1.9. You’ve tested a sample from Illinois for several years in a row, and you continually see that your sample has significantly lower levels than the national average. Thus, if you have strong reason to believe that this year you will again have a sample with lower levels than the national average, you could use a directional hypothesis test.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

For your hypothesis pair you would write the following:

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 = 5.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 < 5.

Again, the difference for a one-tailed test, or a directional hypothesis, is seen in your alternative hypothesis statement: “<” indicates that you hypothesize that scores will be lower than the population mean of 5.

Step 2: Set-up for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? We will use the z-test because we want to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (𝜇).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.
  • Find your critical value(s):zc = −1.65.

Most of this set-up is the same; however, you are testing only one tail. So, your alpha area (0.05) is all on one side of your distribution (see Figure 13.4). So, we need a single critical value to separate our alpha and confidence areas on the side we are testing. In this example, we’ll need a negative critical value to separate our areas. We need to find a z-score that gives us the area beyond z for 0.05. In Table A.1, we see that z = 1.65 gives us that area. So, we will use that z-score, but on the negative side (z = −1.65), to separate our alpha and confidence areas.

Figure 13.4. One-tailed test set-up (hypothesizing that your sample mean is lower than the population mean).

Please note that if you were testing a directional hypothesis where you were hypothesizing that your sample would have higher levels than the norm average, you would use z = 1.65 and mark the alpha area on the positive side of the distribution.

Because your alpha is all on one side of the distribution, that means the alpha area is larger (0.05 on one side versus split into 0.025 on each side). So, the likelihood of rejecting the null hypothesis (i.e., finding a significant difference) increases. However, it is cautioned that if you are not sure where your sample mean will fall, you should conduct a two-tailed test. In our example, what if the sample was taken during 2020–2021, the years of the COVID-19 pandemic? Do you think our sample would have different (or higher) averages, even if they had lower averages for the 5 years prior to this? In these cases where we aren’t sure, and a result may be in the opposite direction of what we’d expect, testing both tails is recommended.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

Your z-obtained calculation remains the same for a directional hypothesis. Let’s look at another year of data: Your sample: x̅ = 4.7, s = 1.7, N = 264; our population data: 𝜇 = 5, 𝜎 = 1.9.

Example 13.1. Calculating Standard Error and z-Obtained Values

Formula for standard error: 

σ x ¯ = σ N

Formula for z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( x ¯ − μ ) σ x ¯

Our example standard error: 

σ x ¯ = 1.9 264 = 0.12

Our example z-obtained value (for the z-test): 

z = ( 4.7 − 5 ) 0.12 = − 2.5

Step 4: Make a Decision

Based on the set-up from Step 2, you’ll see in Figure 13.5 that your z-obtained value (z = −2.5) falls in your alpha area (i.e., it exceeds your critical value of −1.65).

Figure 13.5. Results from hypothesis test showing z-obtained value in the alpha area.

So, you’ll reject the null hypothesis. This means that your sample is significantly lower than the national average, which is what you hypothesized with your one-tailed test.

Let’s go ahead and find our exact p value and maximum confidence level before writing up the results for our report. To find exact p value, we will look up our z-obtained in Table A.1. The area beyond z = 0.0062. We only tested one tail, so our total alpha area = .0062. This is less than (<) 0.05 (our set significance level), so we do have a significant difference. For our maximum confidence level, we will take 1 – alpha, so 1 – 0.0062, which equals 0.9938, or 99.38%. This is greater than 95%, so again, we do have a significant difference.

APA-Style Write-Up

Our American Psychological Association (APA, 2020)-style write-up would be as follows:

A one-sample z-test was calculated to compare the average number of prior incarcerations from a sample of women who are currently incarcerated in Illinois to the mean found with a large, federal survey. Based on a sample size of 264, women in Illinois who were incarcerated had a significantly lower average of prior incarcerations (M = 4.7, SD = 1.9) than the national average (M = 5), z = −2.5, p < .05.

The second sentence could include the exact p value instead of “p < .05”:

Based on a sample size of 264, women in Illinois who were incarcerated had a significantly lower average of prior incarcerations (M = 4.7, SD = 1.9) than the national average (M = 5), z = −2.5, p = .0062.

In both statements, we can indicate that we had a directional hypothesis by also using the phrase “significantly lower” rather than “significantly different.”

To summarize, a directional hypothesis or one-tailed test increases the likelihood of rejecting the null hypothesis or finding a significant difference. This test can be used when expectations of findings are solid. Differences between one-tailed and two-tailed hypothesis tests can be found in the following steps:

  • Alternative hypothesis statement: “<” or “>” rather than “≠”
  • Alpha is still 0.05, but it is not divided between two tails, so the critical value is z = 1.65 (if hypothesized higher) or z = −1.65 (if hypothesized lower) for a one-tailed test. The alpha is all on one side of the distribution.
  • Your exact p value is just the area beyond z. You don’t have to multiply by 2 because you only tested one tail.

Errors in Hypothesis Testing

Another topic in using the hypothesis testing framework is examining errors that can occur. Because we are working with confidence levels (95% or 99%) and we are making inferences based on our level of confidence, there is room for error. For example, with 95% confidence, there is a 5% chance of error. There are two types of error that can occur:

  • First, you have a chance of making a Type I error when you reject the null hypothesis. This is when you say there is a difference, but there actually isn’t a difference. You may see this referred to as a false positive.
  • Second, you have a chance of making a Type II error when you fail to reject the null hypothesis. This is when you say there is no difference, but there actually is a difference. You may see this referred to as a false negative.

You always have the chance of one or the other type of error. As you move the confidence level up (to 99%) or down (to 95%), there’s still a chance of error. Again, you will never have 100% confidence because you are working with samples to make inferences about the populations from which they came. You can try to reduce the amount of sampling error by increasing your sample size (which will reduce your standard error estimate), but you will still have Type I or Type II error to account for. Table 13.1 summarizes hypothesis testing and Type I and II errors.

Table 13.1. Summary of Type I and Type II Errors Based on Hypothesis Testing Conclusion and Reality
When you conclude:

But in reality, there is no relationship, effect, or difference

(i.e., the null is true)

But in reality, there is a significant relationship, effect, or difference

(i.e., the null is false)

“Fail to Reject the Null Hypothesis” (no relationship, effect, or difference)

No error

Type II error

“Reject the Null Hypothesis” (there is a relationship, effect, or difference)

Type I error

No error

Limitations to Hypothesis Testing

Although the hypothesis testing framework is helpful for using inferential statistics and drawing conclusions, there are also limitations worth considering, in addition to the chances of error.

In Step 4 of the hypothesis test we either reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. Let’s look at the following example. We have two samples, and their means are extremely close (M = 101.97 and M = 101.95). When we compare each of these samples to the population mean (M = 100), we would go through the four steps of the hypothesis test to make a conclusion. As you see in the example Comparing Sample 1 and Sample 2, Sample 1 has a z-obtained value of 1.97, and Sample 2 has a z-obtained value of 1.95. These obtained values are very close to each other, but they are on either side of your critical value of 1.96. So, you’d make different decisions about these samples. Thus, it is important to use caution with results f rom hypothesis testing when your obtained values are close to a critical value.

Similarly, if we think about the conclusions we drew from these tests, we would say that Sample 1 has a “significant difference,” whereas Sample 2 “did not have a significant difference.” There are absolute decisions and conclusions based on a small difference between your obtained values and where they fall in relation to your critical value.

Example 13.2. Comparing Sample 1 and Sample 2

Sample 1 (N = 225): x̅ = 101.97, s = 15

  • z-critical value = ±1.96.
  • z-obtained value = 1.97.
  • Reject the null hypothesis: There is a significant difference (i.e., z-obtained value of 1.97 exceeds z-critical value of 1.96).

Sample 2 (N = 225): x̅ = 101.95, s = 15

  • z-critical value = ±1.96.
  • z-obtained value = 1.95.
  • Fail to reject the null hypothesis: There is not a significant difference (i.e., z-obtained value of 1.95 does not exceed z-critical value of 1.96).

In addition, hypothesis tests do not directly address the magnitude of your result. For example, if we have a z-obtained value of 3.2 and a z-obtained value of 16.8, we would make the same inference for both of these obtained values (i.e., we would reject the null hypothesis, stating that there is a significant difference). Thus, although hypothesis testing can be useful, it is important to keep these limitations in mind, especially if you have a marginal result that borders the critical value.

Summary

When you have strong expectations about the direction of your result, you can use directional hypothesis testing (i.e., a one-tailed test), which can increase the likelihood of rejecting the null hypothesis. Differences between one-tailed and two-tailed hypothesis tests can be found in the following steps:

  • Alternative hypothesis statement: “<” or “>” rather than “≠”
  • Alpha is still 0.05, but it is not divided between two tails, so the critical value is 1.65 (if hypothesized higher) or −1.65 (if hypothesized lower) for a one-tailed test.
  • Your exact p value is just the area beyond z. You don’t have to multiply by 2 because you only tested one tail.

When using hypothesis testing, there is a chance for two errors to occur, as well as a few limitations to keep in mind:

  • Type I error: when you reject the null hypothesis when there actually isn’t a difference (false positive).
  • Type II error: when you fail to reject the null hypothesis when there actually is a difference (false negative).
  • Limitations: with an all-or-nothing decision and the inability to address the magnitude of the results, it is important to keep these limitations in mind. Use caution when interpreting and reporting results that fall near a critical value.

V

Unit 5. Inferential Statistics: Looking at Differences

This unit examines four types of inferential statistics that answer research questions around differences. For example, we will be testing differences between two or more groups or differences within participants across time. These tests include three types of t-tests, as well as the analysis of variance (ANOVA). The accompanying table provides a summary of these tests.

Table V.1. Summary of Inferential Statistical Tests and Research Questions in Unit 5

Inferential Statistical Test

Research Question

One-sample t-test

Allows you to compare one sample mean to a population mean (when population standard deviation is unknown and/or you have a small sample)

Independent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences between two independent sample means

Dependent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences within two dependent sample means

Analysis of variance (ANOVA)

Allows you to compare three or more independent sample means (with a one-way ANOVA)

14

Chapter 14: An Introduction to t-Tests and the One-Sample t-test

In previous chapters, we have seen the z-test as our first type of inferential test. We compared one sample mean to a population mean. Our next type of inferential test is the one-sample t-test; this test is very similar to the z-test because we are still comparing one sample mean to a mean of a population. The key differences are what information is known about the population and your sample size. In this chapter, we will first introduce thet-test, which allows us to test inferential hypotheses with smaller samples and when we do not know our population standard deviation. The t-test allows us to calculate the expected sampling error (i.e., standard error) using our sample standard deviation and make adjustments to our analyses based on our sample size. Using a t-test will have impacts on hypothesis testing, including the test you select in Step 2, the critical values you use, and the distribution you use.

The t-Distribution and Degrees of Freedom

The t-test uses the t distribution, which looks very similar to the standard normal distribution (see Figure 14.1). You still have an area of 1.00 under the bell-shaped curve; the mean is still 0 at the center of your distribution. If your sample size is around 100 or greater, the shape of your distribution looks normal (i.e., it approximates the normal distribution). However, if your sample size is smaller (typically less than 100), the shape changes slightly as a function of your degrees of freedom. Thus, t distributions are a family of distributions; each distribution looks slightly different for each different degree of freedom.

Figure 14.1. t Distributions are a family of distributions, that adjust to your degrees of freedom (df).

The term degrees of freedom is defined as the number of observations or values in the data that are free to vary. To illustrate degrees of freedom, let’s say you have seven clients. Across their cognitive assessment scores, the total score was 30. Scores ranged from 2 (low cognitive difficulties) to 6 (high cognitive difficulties). You decide to assign each client to a case manager for follow-ups. To keep things fair, you have case managers pull a client letter out of a bag:

  • Case Manager 1 has seven clients they may get; they pull Client A out of the bag, and this client has a score of 4.
  • Case Manager 2 now has six clients they may get; they pull Client B out of the bag, and this client has a score of 6.
  • Case Manager 3 now has five clients they may get; they pull Client C out of the bag, and this client has a score of 3.
  • Case Manager 4 now has four clients they may get; they pull Client D out of the bag, and this client has a score of 4.
  • Case Manager 5 now has three clients they may get; they pull Client E out of the bag, and this client has a score of 5.
  • Case Manager 6 now has two clients they may get; they pull Client F out of the bag, and this client has a score of 6.
  • Now, Case Manager 7 does not have any “degrees of freedom”; in other words, they only have one client left to pull out of the bag. We would also already know what Client G’s score would be. Again, the total was 30, and if you add the rest of the clients’ scores that were already selected (4 + 6 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 28), you can see that this client’s score is 2. So, although each case manager had client scores that were “free to vary” for Clients A to F, the case manager who gets the final client score would have to be the client with a score of 2.

This example helps illustrate how we find degrees of freedom. Across statistical tests, you may be estimating one parameter, or you may be estimating multiple parameters. So, your calculation of degrees of freedom  will differ depending on your test. However, in this chapter, we will be estimating one parameter (i.e., the population mean with a one-sample t-test). So, to calculate our degrees of freedom, we will use N – 1

Figure 14.2. “Woman Smiling While Looking at her Man” by Marcus Aurelius, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

As you’ll see later in this chapter, we will be using our degrees of freedom calculation ( N – 1 ) t distribution that adjusts for sample size and corresponding degrees of freedom. For example, if your N = 5, your degrees of freedom would be 4 (often notated as df), or df = 4. This distribution would be adjusted for the smaller size compared with a sample where N = 100, with 99 degrees of freedom. If you look at Table A.2 in the Appendix, you’ll see the degrees of freedom listed to help you find the corresponding critical values for your t distribution.

Unlike the z-test, which for 95% confidence could always use z = ±1.96 as the critical values, you’ll need to adjust for sample size and degrees of freedom when using the t-test. Therefore, you’ll need to look up t-test critical values for every hypothesis test you conduct, based on your degrees of freedom (e.g., N − 1

Again, if your sample size is around 100 or greater, the shape of your t distribution approximates the normal distribution shape. Thus, as your sample size (and degrees of freedom) increase, the t distribution approximates the standard normal distribution. You can see this approximation when you look at the critical values for 100 degrees of freedom. With 95% confidence for a two-tailed test, your t-critical values would be ±1.984. These values are close to ±1.96 for z-critical values. When you have 500 degrees of freedom, you’re even closer to approximating the standard normal distribution, with t-critical values of ±1.965.

By adjusting the distribution shape by degrees of freedom, the t distribution adjusts for the likely amount of error that is involved with smaller samples. This variation by degrees of freedom (and corresponding t-critical value[s]) is what allows t-tests to be able to make more accurate inferences; we end up with a more precise estimation.

One-Sample t-Test

The first type of t-test we’ll conduct is a one-sample t-test. This test answers research questions like you asked when using a z-test. However, as shown in the decision tree in Figure 14.3, if you do not know your population mean and standard deviation, and/or you have a small sample size, then you will be using a t-test. As we go through the four steps of the one-sample t-test hypothesis test, the differences for a t-test versus a z-test will be highlighted.

Example: Hypothesis Test of Post-Traumatic Stress Symptoms Among Parents

You are a medical social worker who works in a hospital integrated care unit (for more information on the role of social workers in integrated care, see Milano et al. [2022]). You are assigned to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and are helping assess levels of post-traumatic stress symptoms (PTSS) among parents who had an infant in the NICU. Your unit supervisor wants to know if this sample of parents (N = 35) has different levels of PTSS compared with a norm sample of parents who also experienced similar events.

Research question: Does this sample of parents have different levels of PTSS compared with the norm?

From the assessment manual, you find that 𝜇 = 70. Right away, you might be able to think about the type of test we can use here. There is no population standard deviation provided, and you have a small sample (N = 35). These should be clues that you’ll be running a type of t-test.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

There are no differences in the hypothesis pair statements between one-sample z-tests and t-tests because our research questions are similar (i.e., comparing one sample mean to a population mean). We will be running a two-tailed test in this example, so we will use “≠” in our alternative hypothesis.

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 = 70.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 ≠ 70.

This can also be notated as follows:

  • Ho: μ1 = 70.
  • Ha: μ1 ≠ 70.

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? We will use a one sample t-test. Why? Because we want to compare one sample mean (x̅) to a population mean (μ). However, we do not know our population standard deviation in this example, and we have a small sample size (N = 35). So, we will use a one-sample t-test (instead of the z-test) to test our question.
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.
  • Find your critical value(s): t-critical values (tc)= ±2.032.

To find our t-critical values, we’ll use Table A.2. First, we must calculate our degrees of freedom (df). We will take N – 1 N = 35, so our d f = 35 – 1 = 34

When we find df = 34, our critical value is 2.032. Again, we are testing both tails, so our critical values are ±2.032. See Figure 14.4.

Figure 14.4. Set-up for our one-sample t-test example, with critical values separating our alpha and confidence areas.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

First, solve for the standard error, using your sample standard deviation (8) divided by the square root of your sample size (35). Then, use that value to find your t-obtained value.

Norm sample: 𝜇 = 70.

Your sample: N = 35, x̅ = 74, s = 8.

Formula 14.1. Calculating standard error and t-obtained value for one-sample t-test

Formula for standard error:

s x ¯ = s N

Formula for t-obtained value (for the one-sample t-test):

t = ( x ¯ − μ ) s x ¯

Example 14.1. Calculating Standard Error and t-Obtained Values

Formula for standard error:

s x ¯ = s N

Formula for t-obtained (for the one-sample t-test): 

t = ( x ¯ − μ ) s x ¯

Our example–standard error:

s x ¯ = 8 35 = 1.35

Our example–t-obtained value: 

t = ( 74 − 70 ) 1.35 = 2.96

For our example, the t-obtained value is 2.96.

Figure 14.5. The t-obtained value (t = 2.96) shown on our t distribution that we set-up in Step 2.

Step 4: Make a Decision

As shown in Figure 14.5, if we plot where our t-obtained value (t = 2.96) falls in relation to your confidence and alpha areas (as defined in Step 2), we see that our obtained value falls in the alpha area of the distribution (i.e., it also exceeds our critical value of 2.032). This means that we will reject the null hypothesis. This result means that our sample is significantly different from the population mean; this sample has an average score that falls beyond the confidence area. This book does not include tables for exact p values, but you can compute this using your t-obtained value and degrees of freedom in Excel or through various online calculators (e.g., Social Science Statistics, n.d.). In our example, our exact p value is .006, so p < .05, which also indicates a statistically significant difference.

APA-Style Write-Up

The American Psychological Association (APA, 2020)-style write-up for a one-sample t-test is very similar to that for the z-test. One noted difference is that when you write the t-obtained value, you now include your degrees of freedom in parentheses (in this example, “34”), after the t, and then include the obtained value:

A one-sample t-test was calculated to compare the average levels of PTSS among NICU parents with the norm average. Based on a sample of 35 parents, this sample did have significantly different levels of PTSS (mean [M] = 74, standard deviation [SD] = 8), than the norm average (M = 70), t(34) = 2.96, p < .05.

If you calculate the exact p value, the second sentence could also include the exact p value:

Based on a sample of 35 parents, this sample did have significantly different levels of PTSS (M = 74, SD = 8) than the norm average (M = 70), t(34) = 2.96, p = .006.

Summary

When we do not know our population parameter (𝜎), and we have small sample sizes (N < 100), we can conduct inferential statistics using the t distribution. This is a family of distributions; each distribution looks slightly different for each different degree of freedom. In this chapter, we highlighted the one-sample t-test, which compares a sample mean to a population mean. However, this t-test is unique from the z-test because we do not know our population standard deviation, and we had a small sample size.

15

Chapter 15: Independent Samples t-Tests

In Chapter 14, the t-test, with t distributions based on degrees of freedom, was introduced. Across the next two chapters, we will examine two additional types of t-tests: independent and dependent samples t-tests. Both tests continue to assess research questions that examine differences. To keep our research questions organized, Table 15.1 shows the three types of t-tests and the questions we will test across Chapters 14 to 16.

Table 15.1. Summary of t-Tests and Research Questions

Inferential Statistical Test

Research Question

One-sample t-test

Allows you to compare one sample mean to a population mean (when population standard deviation is unknown and/or you have a small sample)

Independent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences between two independent sample means

Dependent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences within two dependent sample means

Independent Samples t-Test

The independent samples t-test compares means between two samples, each randomly selected from a different population. If you have two independent groups and you want to see if they are significantly different from one another, this is the t-test to use to help answer this question.

Example: Comparing Types of After-School Programming

For example, if you are running an after-school program for young children, you may be curious to compare mean levels of communication skills between those who participate in the theater-based activities (Group 1) and those who participate in sports-based activities (Group 2). For each group, you could calculate a sample mean and then use an independent samples t-test to see if there is a significant difference between these two groups in their levels of communication skills.

As we continue in this book, levels of measurement will become important to assess before selecting an inferential test. By identifying our variables’ levels of measurement, we can then appropriately select the correct inferential test to answer our question. For an independent samples t-test, you will have research questions that have a categorical independent variable, with two groups or samples. Your dependent variable will be continuous (because you will be looking at means). In our example, here is our research question, along with our variables and their levels of measurement identified:

Research question: Are levels of communication skills dependent on the students’ activity group in the after-school program?

  • Independent variable: Activity group type–categorical variable that has two groups: (1) theater-based activities or (2) sports-based activities)
  • Dependent variable: Communication skills–continuous variable with a mean score for each group

The independent samples t-test will examine the mean differences in a variable between two groups. The test will compare a sample mean from each group: Group 1 (x̅1) and Group 2 (x̅2). Both of these groups have their own population means that they are sampled from and making inferences about (μ1 and μ2). We can use a subscript “1” and “2” to identify our two groups. We will be testing a sampling distribution of (x̅1 – x̅2) and testing whether there is a significant difference between two means (see Figure 15.1).

 

Figure 15.1. An independent samples t-test examines the difference between two sample means, making inferences about the population difference.

Let’s go through our example with a full hypothesis test for an independent samples t-test. Here’s some information we’ll need to conduct this hypothesis test (i.e., mean, sum of squares, and sample size for each group). Remember, we use a subscript “1” and “2” with our notation to distinguish information between our two groups.

  • Group 1 (theater-based group): x̅1 = 13.78, SS1 = 310, N1 = 36
  • Group 2 (sports-based group): x̅2 = 11.60, SS2 = 272, N2 = 36

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

We are comparing two sample means, both of which came from their own population. So, we are making inferences about μ1 and μ2, and will refer to them in our hypothesis pair. Our null hypothesis states that the mean of the population from which Sample 1 was selected is equal to the mean of the population from which Sample 2 was selected.

The alternative hypothesis states that the mean of the population from which sample 1 was selected is not equal to or different from the mean of the population from which sample 2 was selected. Your hypothesis pair for an independent samples t-test will always look like this because you are comparing two samples and populations to each other rather than to a comparison value (e.g., population average), in contrast to the z-test and one-sample t-test.

So, your hypothesis pair for an independent samples t-test is as follows:

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 = μ2.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 ≠ μ2.

This can also be written as follows:

  • H0: μ1 = μ2.
  • Ha: μ1 ≠ μ2.

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? Independent samples t-test
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves testing mean differences between two independent groups.
      • You have a categorical independent variable with two groups (theater-based versus sports-based activity groups) and a continuous dependent variable (mean levels of communication).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.

Before we finish step 2 by finding our critical values, we first must review the two types of independent samples t-tests: one that assumes the two population variances are equal (i.e., pooled variance t-test) and one that does not assume the population variances are equal (i.e.,separate variance t-test or Welch’s t-test). There is an F-test (testing σ 1 2 = σ 2 2  to  σ 1 2 ≠ σ 2 2 t-test would be fine to use). However, when sample sizes differ and you want a more conservative estimate to account for each group’s variance, then the separate variance t-test is recommended.

The process of finding your degrees of freedom (which then will help you find your critical values) will differ depending on which independent samples t-test you select. For calculating the degrees of freedom with a pooled variance t-test, we take away 1 degree of freedom for each sample we have. Because we have two samples in this type of test, we will take away 2 degrees of freedom: d f = ( N 1 + N 2 ) − 2

Formula 15.1. Calculating degrees of freedom (pooled variance t-test)

Formula for degrees of freedom (df; pooled variance t-test):

d f = ( N 1 + N 2 ) − 2

You’ll add the sample size from Group 1 (N1) and the sample size from Group 2 (N2). Then, you’ll subtract 2 degrees of freedom. You’ll use this value to look up your critical values in Table A.2.

In our example, N1 = 36, and N2 = 36.

Example 15.1. Calculating Degrees of Freedom (Pooled Variance t-Test)

Formula for degrees of freedom (df; pooled variance t-test):

d f = ( N 1 + N 2 ) − 2

Our example: 

d f = ( 36 + 36 ) − 2 = 70

In Table A.2, df = 70 gives us a t-critical value of ±1.994. This gives you what you need for the third part of Step 2 if you are running a pooled variance independent samples t-test (see Figure 15.2):

  • Find your critical value(s):tc = ±1.994.
Figure 15.2. Setup for our independent samples t-test example.

For a separate variance t-test, your equation for finding the degrees of freedom is more complicated, often producing a noninteger value. The website Stats Kingdom will calculate your degrees of freedom for you.

In our example, df = 69.70. This would round up to 70 when looking up your critical values in Table A.2, so you would have the same critical values, tc = 1.994.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

To calculate your t-obtained value for an independent samples t-test, you first need to conduct an F-test for variance. If you found that your variances were significantly different, then you would run a separate variance t-test. If you found that your variances were not significantly different, then you would run a pooled variance t-test. In this book, the F-test is not shown. Again, when the group sample sizes are equal or very similar in size, variances are likely to be equal (and a pooled variance t-test would be fine to use). However, when sample sizes differ and you want a more conservative estimate to account for each group’s variance, then the separate variance t-test is recommended. Many software programs that calculate independent samples t-tests (e.g., Excel, SPSS) give you results for both pooled and separate variance t-tests that you can choose from.

The steps and formulas for the pooled and separate variance independent samples t-tests are shown here for your reference.

Formula 15.2. Calculating pooled variance t-test

Steps and formulas for pooled variance t-test:

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2 s p 2 = ( S S 1 + S S 2 ) ( d f 1 + d f 2 )
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = s p 2 N 1 + s p 2 N 2
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 ) s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2
Formula 15.3. Calculating separate variance t-test

Steps and formulas for separate variance t-test

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2 s 1 2 = S S 1 d f 1 s 2 2 = S S 2 d f 2
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = s 1 2 N 1 + s 2 2 N 2
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 ) s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2

First, you will calculate variance or variances. For the pooled variance t-test, you are combining information from both samples for a “pooled” variance. For separate variance t-test, you are calculating variance for each sample separately, so you’ll end up with two variance values (one for each sample).

Second, you’ll use these variance estimates to calculate your standard error of the sampling distribution of the difference between means; the notation for this standard error is: s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2

Third, you will look at the difference between your two sample means ( x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 ) t-obtained value.

Let’s calculate a t-obtained value with both methods using our example:

  • Group 1 (theater-based group): x̅1 = 13.78, SS1 = 310, N1 = 36.
  • Group 2 (sports-based group): x̅2 = 11.60, SS2 = 272, N2 = 36.
Example 15.2. Calculating t-Obtained Value with the Pooled Variance t-Test

Steps and formulas for pooled variance t-test:

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2 s p 2 = ( S S 1 + S S 2 ) ( d f 1 + d f 2 )
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = s p 2 N 1 + s p 2 N 2
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 ) s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2

Our example: 

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2 s p 2 = ( 310 + 272 ) ( 35 + 35 ) = 8.31
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = 8.31 36 + 8.31 36 = 0.68
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( 13.78 − 11.60 ) 0.68 = 3.21
Example 15.3. Calculating t-Obtained Value with the Separate Variance t-Test

Steps and formulas for separate variance t-test:

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2 s 1 2 = S S 1 d f 1 s 2 2 = S S 2 d f 2
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = s 1 2 N 1 + s 2 2 N 2
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 ) s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2

Our example: 

  1. Calculate variance (pooled, s p 2 s 1 2 s 2 2   s 1 2 = 310 35 = 8.86 s 2 2 = 272 35 = 7.77
  2. Find your standard error ( s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2   s x ¯ 1 − x ¯ 2 = 8.86 36 + 7.77 36 = 0.68
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = ( 13.78 − 11.60 ) 0.68 = 3.21

You end up with the same t-obtained value (see Figure 15.3). If you were comparing two samples with different sample sizes, then you would likely see different t-obtained values. The separate variance test will give you a more conservative estimate, adjusting for each sample’s variance.

Figure 15.3. The t-obtained (t = 3.21) is marked on our t distribution.

Step 4: Make a Decision

Based on this example, you would then make a decision to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. In both the pooled and separate variance t-tests, you would reject the null hypothesis. Your obtained value (regardless of whether you use the pooled or separate variance tests) exceeds the critical value and is in the alpha area. This means that there is a significant difference in communication skills between children who participate in the theater group compared with the sports group in the after-school program.

APA-Style Write-up

For your American Psychological Association [APA]-style write-up, you will include information about the sample means you are comparing, and again, because you’re using the t distribution, you will include information about your degrees of freedom:

An independent samples t-test was conducted to compare communication skills between those who participated in the theater-based activity group and those who participated in the sports-based activity group. There was a significant difference between those who participated in the theater-based activity group (mean [M] = 13.78) and those who participated in the sports-based activity group (M = 11.60), t(70) = 3.21, p < .05.

Summary

This chapter introduced the independent samples t-test. With this type of test, you have a categorical independent variable (with two independent groups) and a continuous dependent variable, and you are looking at mean differences. There are two types of independent samples t-tests, pooled and separate variance t-tests, which allow you to compare two groups regardless of whether they are similar in size or not.
