Chapter 16: Dependent Samples t-test

In Chapters 14 and 15, we saw two types of t-tests: the one-sample t-test and the independent samples t-test. This chapter introduces our final type in this book, which is called the dependent samples t-test. As a reminder, Table 16.1 summarizes the three types of t-tests and the research questions they can answer.

Table 16.1. Summary of t-Tests and Research Questions

Inferential Statistical Test

Research Question

One-sample t-test

Allows you to compare one sample mean to a population mean (when population standard deviation is unknown and/or you have a small sample)

Independent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences between two independent sample means

Dependent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences within two dependent sample means

Dependent Samples t-Test

The dependent samples t-test, sometimes referred to as a paired samples t-test, is when you compare two dependent sample means. These samples are dependent because they come from some type of pair: two samples of scores from the same person (i.e., so their second score is dependent on their first) or two samples of scores from the same couple (e.g., a married couple’s score is dependent on each of the partners’ scores). Thus, we want to compare means within two groups or samples that are dependent to see if they are significantly different from each other.

One of the most common applications of this test in social work is using this test for a pre-/posttest research design. These designs include a Time 1 pretest (sometimes called a baseline assessment), participation in some type of intervention, and then a Time 2 posttest (sometimes called a follow-up assessment). You have the same people in both samples (Time 1 sample and Time 2 sample), and you then compare their pairs of scores (e.g., do we see increases in scores from Time 1 to Time 2 for each participant?). Thus, the overall goal of dependent samples t-tests is to examine mean differences within a pair of scores.

Example: Evaluating a Parenting Program

A group of clinical social workers is implementing a parenting program in which participants learn parenting strategies and skills. The social workers are interested in finding out whether parents show a significant change in their parent-child relationship quality because of this program. All participants receive a parenting practices scale that assesses parent-child relationship quality; scores range from 0 (poor quality) to 50 (strong quality). Conducting a dependent samples t-test will allow you to answer the following research question: Do parents who participate in the parenting program show improvements in their parent-child relationship quality from Time 1 (before they participate in the program) to Time 2 (after they participate in the program)?

Research methods courses will highlight an array of other research designs that allow you to keep testing these types of program evaluation questions. However, most program evaluations in the setting of community-based organization start with this pre-/posttest research design.

Figure 16.1. “A Happy Family Sitting on the Grass” by RDNE Stock project, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

Let’s look at our level of measurement for our variables in this example. For a dependent samples t-test, you will have research questions that have a categorical independent variable, with two dependent groups or samples. Your dependent variable will be continuous (because you will be looking at means). In our example, here is our research question, with variables and their levels of measurement identified:

Research question: Do parents who participate in the parenting program show improvements in their parent-child relationship quality from Time 1 (before they participate in the program) to Time 2 (after they participate in the program)?

  • Independent variable: Time (the two categories are Time 1 and Time 2)
  • Dependent variable: Parenting skills (continuous variable with a mean score for each time point)

With a pre-/posttest design, your outcome depends on time. You may hypothesize that participants at Time 2 (after participation) would have significantly different levels of parenting skills than they did at Time 1 (before participation).

Note: If you were to conduct a dependent samples t-test with other paired data, you might have your independent variable be “Couple,” with Partner 1 and Partner 2 as your two categories.

Before we examine the hypothesis test for the dependent samples t-test, let’s look at the data for our example, as shown in Table 16.2. This will highlight a key element of this test, which is to account for the dependence of the data.

These data are dependent, in that you have paired data: The Time 1 and Time 2 scores that you are comparing are from within the same person. For example, Participant A scored 36 at Time 1 and 40 at Time 2. Participant F had a score of 25 at Time 1 and 39 at Time 2. These differences within a person are what we are interested in testing. So, the inferences related to differences are for the population mean at Time 1 ( μ A μ B x A − x B μ A − μ B μ A − μ B μ D

Figure 16.2. We will take samples from paired data (A and B), both of which come from their own population.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

We are comparing two dependent sample means, both of which came from their own population, so we are making inferences about 𝜇A and 𝜇B and referring to them in our hypothesis pair. Because our means are dependent, we are interested in the difference within each pair, so we will be referring to difference scores (D) throughout the hypothesis test. So, you’ll have options for writing your hypothesis pair.

Our null hypothesis states that the difference between the paired sample means is equal to 0. The two samples (from a pair) came from a population where the mean difference was 0. You’ll compare this hypothesis to the alternative hypothesis, which would state that the difference between the paired sample means was not equal to 0. The paired sample came from a population where the mean difference was not 0. Your hypothesis pair for dependent samples t-test will always look like this:

  • Null hypothesis: μA – μB = 0.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μA – μB ≠ 0.

This can also be written as follows:

  • H0: μA – μB = 0.
  • Ha: μA – μB ≠ 0.

The other ways you can write your hypothesis pairs refer to the difference scores with “D” as the notation:

  • Null hypothesis: μD = 0.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μD ≠ 0.

This can also be written as follows:

  • H0: μD = 0.
  • Ha: μD ≠ 0.

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? Dependent samples t-test
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves testing differences within paired sample or dependent means (i.e., means from the same person).
      • You have a categorical independent variable with two groups (Time 1 and Time 2) and a continuous dependent variable (mean levels of parent-child relationship quality).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05. 

Finding your degrees of freedom will then set you up for determining your critical values. You will take N, or your total sample size, and subtract 1 ( N − 1

Formula 16.1. Calculating degrees of freedom (dependent samples t-test)

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) for dependent samples t-test:

d f = N – 1

Example 16.1. Calculating Degrees of Freedom for Dependent Samples t-Test

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) for dependent samples t-test:

d f = N – 1

Our example: 

d f = 10 − 1 = 9

In Table A.2, df = 9 gives us a t-critical value of ±2.262. This gives what we need for the third part of our Step 2:

  • Find your critical value(s): tc = ±2.262 (see Figure 16.3).
Figure 16.3. Set-up for dependent samples t-test.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

To find our t-obtained value for a dependent samples t-test, we will again focus on the differences within pairs: D = x A − x B

Formula 16.2. Calculating t-obtained value for dependent samples t-test

Steps and formulas for calculating dependent samples t-test:

  1. Calculate average differences between paired scores:  x ¯ D = ∑ D N D ¯ = ∑ D N
  2. Find your standard error:  s x ¯ D = s D N s D ¯ = s D N
  3. Solve for t-obtained value:  t = x ¯ D s x ¯ D t = D ¯ s D ¯

Let’s pull our data table here and add a few columns to help us get the values we need for these equations, as well as a summary row at the bottom (see Table 16.3). The fourth column includes the difference score for each pair. Because we are interested in differences within a pair of scores (i.e., difference between Time 1 and Time 2 score for each participant), we will first calculate these scores for each participant. For example, Participant A scored 36 (Time 1) and then 40 (Time 2); this difference score is −4. The bottom row of the “Difference Score” column adds all of the difference scores; we’ll use that value in calculating the average differences between paired scores. Let’s do that calculation first; we will return to the fifth column after we calculate the average differences between paired scores.

So, first we will calculate the average difference ( D ¯ −36) and divide by the number of participants (or pairs of scores, which is 10) that we have. This tells that on average, there was a difference within participants of −3.6 points on the parent-child relationship quality assessment from Time 1 to Time 2. We will also use this value in our third equation of this step to solve for the t-obtained value.

Example 16.2. Calculating the Average Difference

Formula for average difference:

x ¯ D = ∑ D N

also written as:

D ¯ = ∑ D N

Our example: 

x ¯ D = − 36 10 = − 3.6

also written as:

D ¯ = − 36 10 = − 3.6

Now that we know the average difference score was −3.6, we can use this in our calculation to find the standard error of the difference scores. The fifth column of the table takes each participant’s difference score, minus the average of our difference scores (−3.6, which we just calculated in our first step), squared, in the equation for the standard error. For example, Participant A had a difference score of −4, so we take − 4 – ( − 3.6 ) = − 0.4

Again, along the bottom of the table is a summary row, where we have average scores at Time 1 and Time 2, as well as sums of our difference scores and our squared difference scores.

Next, we will find the standard error of the difference scores. Before we can solve for the standard error of the difference scores, we have to calculate the standard deviation of the difference scores. If this is not provided to you, here’s how you would find this value: You would first take the variance (the sum of difference scores minus average difference score squared and divided by N – 1). Then, to find the standard deviation, take the square root of this value.

Example 16.3. Calculating Standard Deviation of Difference Scores

Formula for standard deviation of difference scores: 

s D = ( ∑ D 2 N − 1 )

Our example: 

s D = ( 192.4 9 ) = 4.62

Example 16.4. Calculating Standard Error of Difference Scores

Formula for standard error of difference scores:

s x ¯ D = s D N

also written as:

s D ¯ = s D N

Our example: 

s x ¯ D = 4.62 10 = 1.46

also written as:

s D ¯ = 4.62 10 = 1.46

Then, to find the standard error, you’ll take the standard deviation of the difference scores (4.62) and divide by the square root of N, which in this case is 10. So, your standard error of the difference scores is 1.46.

Finally, you have the information you need to solve for your t-obtained value. You will take your average difference score and divide it by your standard error of the difference scores.

Example 16.5. Calculating t-Obtained Value

Formula for t-obtained value: 

t = x ¯ D s x ¯ D

also written as:

t = D ¯ s D ¯

Our example: 

t = − 3.6 1.46 = − 2.47

also written as:

t = − 3.6 1.46 = − 2.47

From this equation, your t-obtained value is −2.47 (see Figure 16.4).

Figure 16.4. Our t-obtained value is shown on our t distribution.

Step 4: Make a Decision

Based on this example, you would then make a decision to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. Your t-obtained value falls in the alpha area, so you would reject the null hypothesis. Your obtained value exceeds the critical value and is in the alpha area. This means that there is a significant difference within participants from Time 1 to Time 2 on levels of parent-child relationship quality.

Often you are looking at differences within people from Time 1 to Time 2. If this is the case, keep the following in mind:

  • Negative t-obtained value: This means that Time 2 has higher scores than Time 1. In our example, we would want to see higher scores at Time 2 because this would mean they showed improvements in their relationship quality from Time 1 to Time 2.
  • Positive t-obtained value: This means that Time 2 has lower scores than Time 1. You might want to see this if you’re measuring an adverse outcome, such as depressive symptoms. You’d want to see declines in scores at Time 2 from Time 1, so a positive, significant, t-obtained value would help you interpret that as an impactful program.

APA-Style Write-up

The American Psychological Association [APA]-style write-up for a dependent samples t-test follows; you’ll report your average levels at Time 1 and Time 2, even though you don’t use these means in any of the equations. However, this descriptive information can still be helpful in understanding your sample.

A dependent samples t-test was conducted to compare levels of parent-child relationship quality from pretest (Time 1) to posttest (Time 2) within clients who participated in a parenting program. Based on a sample of 10 clients, individuals showed significantly higher relationship quality at posttest (mean [M] = 40.9) than at pretest (M = 37.3), t(9) = −2.47, p < .05. These findings suggest that the parenting program was effective in improving parent-child relationship quality.

Summary

This chapter introduced the dependent samples t-test, which examines difference scores within paired data (e.g., Time 1 and Time 2 scores from the same person). This is a common t-test when social workers use a pre-/posttest research design to evaluate a program or intervention.

17

Chapter 17: (One-Way) Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

Our final type of inferential statistic that looks at differences in this book is the analysis of variance, or ANOVA. We will be focusing on the one-way ANOVA, which examines differences between the means of three or more groups or categories (of one independent variable) and one dependent variable. More advanced statistics books will highlight other types of ANOVAs, where you can have multiple independent and/or dependent variables.

One-Way ANOVA

The one-way ANOVA examines differences between three or more categories of one independent variable on a continuous dependent variable. Research questions are very similar to those of an independent variable t-test (Chapter 15); the key difference is the number of levels, or categories of your independent variable. If you have two levels, you can use the independent samples t-test; if you have three or more levels, then you can use the one-way ANOVA.

Example: Comparing Conflict Resolution Skills of Participants in Restorative Justice Programs

Let’s say you are interested in comparing levels of conflict resolution skills among youth who participate in one of three types of evidence-based restorative justice programs (for more information on restorative justice programs, please see Kimbrell et al. [2022] for a review). Your team collects youth self-reported conflict resolution skills after they participate in the program. You end up with a mean for each of the three groups: x̅1, x̅2, and x̅3. Because you have three levels in this example (i.e., three independent programs), you would conduct an ANOVA.

Figure 17.1. “Man Showing a Document on a Woman” by Felicity Tai, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

In this example, you now have three comparisons: Program 1 to Program 2, Program 1 to Program 3, and Program 2 to Program 3. You might be wondering why you can’t just run multiple t-tests for each of these comparisons. However, with every t-test, you would increase the risk for a Type I error (see Chapter 13). Across comparisons, you would increase your overall chance of error (also called experiment-wise alpha, which is the probability of making a Type I error across multiple tests). For example, if you had 95% confidence level set for each test, you would then have a 5% chance of error for each comparison:

  1. Comparing Program 1 to Program 2: 5% error
  2. Comparing Program 1 to Program 3: 5% error
  3. Comparing Program 2 to Program 3: 5% error

This would result in a total of 15% error across the three comparisons.

Luckily, ANOVA and additional tests conducted after the initial ANOVA (e.g., post hoc tests), allow you to make these comparisons, while keeping your alpha level at the specified level (e.g., 0.05, or 5%), thus controlling your experiment-wise alpha.

The logic of the ANOVA test examines the total variability within a data set and then partitions the sources of variability: (1) between each group, and (2) within each group. Between-group variability examines differences between the group means. This measures how much each group mean differs from the overall mean (across all groups). Within-group variability examines variability within each group; this variability accounts for the error that each group contributes. Each group is examined separately for the amount of within-group variability it contributes; if there are large variance estimates, there is more room for error, and it makes it harder to detect between group differences because there is more variability within groups.

Our obtained value is F, which is the ratio of between-group to within-group variability.

F = v a r i a n c e b e t w e e n g r o u p s v a r i a n c e w i t h i n g r o u p s

If the ratio is large, then there is more variability between groups, which indicates more of an effect or difference between groups. If the ratio is small, then there is less of a difference, and there is more room for error within a group. If the ratio is 1, then the groups are roughly the same (i.e., the variance between and variance within groups are roughly the same; any differences you can see are likely due to chance).

Because F values are a ratio, they are always positive. The F value that we will calculate in an ANOVA hypothesis test will be plotted using the F distribution, which is scaled by variance rather than standard deviation like the t distribution and standard normal distribution. Thus, the distribution starts at 0, peaks at 1, and then extends a tail for positive critical and obtained values. Like the t distribution, the F distribution is also a family of distributions, where the characteristics and shape vary according to degrees of freedom (see Figure 17.2).

Figure 17.2. The F distribution.

Because we are partitioning the variability for ANOVA, we will have two sources of degrees of freedom: degrees of freedom within groups and degrees of freedom between groups. We will use these two sources of degrees of freedom when looking up our positive critical value (see Table A.3 in the Appendix).

Formula 17.1. Calculating degrees of freedom (df) for between and within groups

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) between groups: 

k – 1

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) within groups: 

N t – k

To find degrees of freedom between groups, you will take k (which is the number of levels or groups you are examining) and subtract 1. To find degrees of freedom within groups, you will take your total N (across all groups, notated as Nt) and subtract k.

Let’s continue our example comparing conflict resolution skills among participants in one of three restorative justice programs.

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

Your hypothesis pair for a one-way ANOVA will include a null hypothesis where all your group means are equal. Your ratios of between-to-within variability are expected to be similar. You will compare that hypothesis to the alternative hypothesis, where your group means are not equal. This hypothesis suggests that your sample means differ by more than just sampling error; there is a meaningful difference between your group means.

In our example, we are comparing three programs, so our hypothesis pair will look like this:

  • Null hypothesis: μ1 = μ2 = μ3.
  • Alternative hypothesis: μ1 ≠ μ2 ≠ μ3.

You can also notate your hypotheses as follows:

  • H0: μ1 = μ2 = μ3.
  • Ha: μ1 ≠ μ2 ≠ μ3.

These hypothesis statements should remind you of the independent samples t-test statements; they just add the third category or level to the statements because you are now comparing three levels.

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? One-way ANOVA
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves testing mean differences between three levels (i.e., three programs).
      • You have a categorical independent variable with three levels (Program 1, Program 2, Program 3) and a continuous dependent variable (mean levels of conflict resolution skills).
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.

To find our critical value, we need to find our degrees of freedom first. You will have just one critical value, which will be positive, because we are using the F distribution.

For our example, we have three levels, so k = 3. Across the three groups in this example, we have a total of 15 participants, so Nt = 15.

Example 17.1. Calculating Degrees of Freedom Between and Within Groups

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) between groups: 

k – 1

Our example: 

3 – 1 = 2

 

Formula for degrees of freedom (df) within groups: 

N t – k

Our example: 

15 – 3 = 12

So, we will use df between groups  = 2 and df within groups = 12 to look up our F-critical value in Table A.3. With a significance level of 0.05, we look up our degrees of freedom between groups along the top column and then use the degrees of freedom within groups along the left-hand first column. This shows us that our critical value is 3.89. We will use this value to separate our confidence and alpha areas on the F distribution.

  • Find your critical value: Fc = 3.89. 

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

We will use a summary table to help us find all the pieces we need for our F-obtained value (see Table 17.1). The summary table is useful for illustrating our total variability (bottom row), and how we partition our variability into between-groups (top row) and within-groups (middle row) variability. Then we have columns for sum of squares (SS), degrees of freedom (df), mean square (MS), and F (your obtained value).

Step 4: Make a Decision

Based on this example, you would then make a decision to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. In this example, you would reject the null hypothesis. Your obtained value exceeds the critical value and is in the alpha area. This means that there is a significant difference in conflict resolution skills between youth who participate in these three different groups.

APA-Style Write-up

The American Psychological Association ([APA], 2020)-style write-up is similar to that for the independent samples t-test. The key difference is that you are referring to the F-test, as well as your between- and within-groups degrees of freedom.

A one-way ANOVA was conducted to compare the effect of three restorative justice programs on levels of conflict resolution skills. The three conditions were Program 1, Program 2, and Program 3. There was a significant effect of the restorative justice program on youth conflict resolution skills for the three conditions, F(2, 12) = 4.52, p < .05.

Note that for your degrees of freedom in the write-up, you include both your between-groups (2) and within-groups (12) degrees of freedom. The hypothesis test tells us that there is an overall significant effect. However, you may be curious where the difference is: Is it between Programs 1 and 2? Or Programs 1 and 3? Or Programs 2 and 3? This is where the next part of ANOVA comes into play: the post hoc test.

ANOVA Post Hoc Test

Post hoc (Latin for “after this”) tests allow you to find where the difference exists after you get a significant overall test (with the F-test). The post hoc test will show you which groups are significantly different from each other. There is an array of post hoc tests to choose from, depending on your group sizes, the level of confidence you want, and so forth. This book examines one of the most common, which is used when you have an equal number of participants in each group. This post hoc test is called Tukey’s honestly significant difference (HSD) test. In our example, we have five participants in each level, so we can use the Tukey HSD test to find which programs are significantly different from each other. A bar chart could be a useful image to include to help readers understand the comparisons of means when writing about ANOVA results in a report (see Figure 17.4).

Figure 17.4. Bar graph comparing means across the three programs (each program is independent of the others, so each color represents a unique program).

This post hoc test will allow us to make pairwise comparisons:

  • Program 1 versus Program 2
  • Program 1 versus Program 3
  • Program 2 versus Program 3

To find where your difference or differences exist, you will calculate the HSD. The HSD will give you a critical value; if the difference between two of your group means exceeds this critical value, then there is a significant difference between the two means.

Formula 17.2. Calculating Tukey’s HSD

Formula for Tukey’s HSD: 

HSD = q M S within N

If we look at this formula, we’ll notice the following elements:

  • The q value is found in a q-table (known as a Studentized Range Distribution Table; Zaiontz, n.d.). You will look up your q value based on your alpha level, the number of groups you are comparing (k), and your degrees of freedom within groups. A q table is available from Real Statistics Using Excel.
  • In our example, we will find the table for alpha = 0.05, then use the k = 3 column, and the row for df within groups = 12. So, the q value in our example is 3.773.
  • MSwithin has previously been calculated and can be found in your ANOVA summary table. In our example, this value is 7.
  • N is the sample size of any group because the Tukey HSD test is used when your group sizes are the same. So, you’ll use N = 5 in our example.

Example 17.2. Calculating Tukey’s HSD

Formula for Tukey’s HSD: 

HSD = q M S within N

Our example: 

HSD = 3.773 7 5 = 4.45

So, our Tukey HSD value is ±4.45, which is used as a critical value. We will take the mean differences between each group and if the difference exceeds this critical value, then we know whether there is a significant difference between that pairwise comparison. Here are our three means to compare: x̅1 = 8, x̅2 = 6, and x̅3 = 3. 

After you calculate the difference between program means (middle column in Table 17.7), you’ll determine whether that difference exceeds the HSD critical value. If it does, you’ll indicate a significant difference (“p < .05”). In our example, Program 1 versus 3 has a difference of 5 points; 5 exceeds 4.45, so this difference is significant. Our other comparisons have differences of 2 and 3; neither exceeds 4.45, so they are not significantly different (“p > .05”).

APA-Style Write-up

We can now add the information from our post hoc test to our APA-style write-up:

A one-way ANOVA was conducted to compare the effect of three restorative justice programs on levels of conflict resolution skills. The three conditions were Program 1, Program 2, and Program 3. There was a significant effect of the restorative justice program on youth conflict resolution skills for the three conditions, F(2, 12) = 4.52, p < .05.

A Tukey HSD post hoc analysis was used to determine which programs were different. The results of this test indicated that youth who participated in Program 1 had significantly higher levels of conflict resolution skills (mean [M] = 8) than youth who participated in Program 3 (M = 3). No other significant differences were found.

Summary

ANOVA is useful when you want to compare means for three or more groups. ANOVA, using the F distribution, allow you to control experiment-wise alpha by partitioning your variance. The ANOVA hypothesis test tells you if there is an overall significant difference between your groups or not. If there is a significant difference between them, you can follow with a post hoc test. Although there are many options for post hoc tests, the Tukey HSD can be used if your groups are the same size.

N t k” and “i = 1” means that you will repeat the equation for each group, starting with Group 1, and then add these values together.

VI

Unit 6. Inferential Statistics: Looking at Relationships

The final unit in this book examines inferential statistics that look at relationships between variables. We will first examine correlation, specifically correlation between two continuous variables (using Pearson’s r). Following correlation, we will examine the basics of linear regression. Finally, we will examine relationships between categorical data using chi-square tests.

18

Chapter 18: Correlation (Pearson’s r)

Correlation

A correlation is the degree of a linear relationship between two continuous variables. A linear relationship is one that can be described by a straight line. Correlation allows you to visualize the pattern in bivariate data, examining how the variables move together: Do they move in the same direction or in opposite directions? Or maybe the variables do not have a significant relationship; when you look at the data, it is difficult to draw a line to describe their relationship.

Correlation provides you with an estimate of covariance, which is a measure of how two variables move. Correlation between two continuous variables can be tested using Pearson’s r. This test provides you with a value, referred to as the correlation coefficient, between −1 and 1.

First, variables may have a positive value, or apositive correlation (Pearson’s r value between >0 and 1). These variables move in the same direction:

  • As one variable increases, the other variable increases.
  • As one variable decreases, the other variable decreases.

A perfect positive correlation forms a line; a high positive correlation has scattered data points, but you can visualize drawing a line to describe how these data points are moving together, as shown in Figure 18.1.

Figure 18.1. Scatterplot graphs showing a perfect positive correlation and a strong positive correlation.

Second, variables may have a negative value, or a negative correlation (Pearson’s r value between –1 and <0). These variables move in an inverse, or in the opposite, direction:

  • As one variable increases, the other variable decreases.
  • As one variable decreases, the other variable increases.

A perfect negative correlation forms a line; a high negative correlation has scattered data points, but you can visualize drawing a line to describe how these data points are moving together, as shown in Figure 18.2.

Figure 18.2. Scatterplot graphs showing a perfect negative correlation and a strong negative correlation.

Third, variables may haveno correlation (Pearson’s r value of 0), which means that there is no meaningful relationship between the two variables. The data points are scattered, and it is difficult to draw a line to represent how these variables are moving together, as shown in Figure 18.3.

Figure 18.3. A scatterplot graph where there is no relationship between two variables. The data points do not show any linear pattern.

As you can see from these descriptions, Pearson’s r values help describe direction and magnitude:

  • Negative value (between –1 and <0): Tells you the variables are moving in opposite directions; the closer the value is to –1, the stronger the magnitude. A correlation of –1 is a perfect negative correlation.
  • Positive value (between >0 and 1): Tells you the variables are moving in the same direction; the closer the value is to 1, the stronger the magnitude. A correlation of 1 is a perfect positive correlation.
  • A value of 0: There is no correlation between the variables.

An important note about correlation is that these correlations do not imply causation. We can see if the variables move together in the same direction or in opposite directions, but we do not know whether one variable is causing the other variable to move in this way. A common example to illustrate that correlation does not imply causation is that there is a correlation between ice cream sales and violent behavior. If you plotted these data, you’d see that as ice cream sales go up, violent behavior also goes up. These variables are correlated. However, we cannot say that eating more ice cream makes someone commit more violent acts. Nor can we say that violence makes someone eat more ice cream. In this example, the variables are correlated, but a third variable is likely the “cause” of the increase in these variables. That third variable is heat. When it is hot outside, people tend to eat more ice cream. When it is hot outside, we often see rates of violence increase (Anderson, 1989).

However, if you can establish an initial correlation between two variables, this may prompt you to conduct further inferential tests to learn more about the relationship. You may choose research designs that allow you to test cause and effect, ruling out other variables that could have explained or affected the relationship.

Example: Correlation Between Forms of Victimization

To illustrate the hypothesis test and calculate Pearson’s r for a correlation, we will examine the relationship between peer victimization and dating violence victimization among middle school students. A violence prevention practitioner collects data on these forms of violence from nine students. For more on violence prevention programs, see Banyard and Hamby (2022). Both assessments are continuous levels of measurement (i.e., they count the number of incidents for both types of victimization; scores range from 0 to 12 victimization experiences).

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

For our hypothesis pair, we will be using the Greek letter rho (ρ) to represent the population correlation. Because we are still making inferences, we will be writing our hypothesis pair about the population correlation. Our null hypothesis states that there is no correlation (which is a value of 0); our alternative hypothesis states that the correlation is not equal to 0:

  • Null Hypothesis: ρ = 0.
  • Alternative Hypothesis: ρ ≠ 0.

This can also be written as follows:

  • H0: ρ = 0.
  • Ha: ρ ≠ 0.

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? Correlation (Pearson’s r)
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves examining the association between two continuous variables.
      • You have two continuous variables.
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.

To find your critical values, you will use Table A.4 in the Appendix.  Although you are calculating a correlation value using Pearson’s r test, you are still plotting the critical values and obtained value on a t distribution bell-shaped curve. The center of this distribution is 0, which indicates zero correlation.

To look up your critical values, you will use your sample size (N) or your degrees of freedom (df). You’ll notice that in Table A.4 that both N and df are listed in the first two columns. Because Pearson’s r examines the association between two variables, you will always need take N – 2

In our example, we have nine people in our sample, so we can look up N = 9 or we can look up df = 7.

  • Find critical values: r = ±0.666.

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

To find our Pearson’s r (obtained value), we will use the data in Table 18.1. We have two variables, and we assign “x” and “y” to the variables; remember, we are not making causal claims, so you can assign either letter to either variable. The bottom row of Table 18.1 includes some summary information, including the sample size (N = 9), the sum of x, and the sum of y.

The following example works through the steps with our data.

Example 18.1. Calculating Sum of Squares, Sum of Products, and Obtained Value for Correlation

Steps and formulas for calculating obtained value (Pearson’s r): 

  1. Calculate the sum of squares for x

    S S x = ∑ x 2 − ( ∑ x ) 2 N

    Calculate the sum of squares for y

    S S y = ∑ y 2 − ( ∑ y ) 2 N

Our example:

So, in our example, r = 0.97, which is our obtained value. We’ll plot this data point on our distribution and examine it in relation to our critical values.

We can also describe our correlation based on this Pearson’s r. First, it is a positive number, so we have a positive correlation. This means that as one variable increases, the other variable increases; the variables are moving in the same direction. Second, it is closer to 1 than to 0. This tells about the magnitude of the association. An r of 0.97 is very close to 1.00, so the linear relationship is strong; if we impose a line on a scatterplot of the data, the data points are very close to that line, as shown in Figure 18.5.

Figure 18.5. Scatterplot graph showing peer victimization and dating violence victimization with a line imposed.

Step 4: Make a Decision

Based on this example, you would then make a decision to reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis. In this example, you would reject the null hypothesis. Your obtained value (r = .97) exceeds the critical value (±0.666) and is in the alpha area (see Figure 18.6). This means that there is a significant (and positive) correlation between peer victimization and dating violence victimization.

Figure 18.6. Distribution with critical values shown, as well as the obtained value of .97.

APA-Style Write-Up

The American Psychological Association ([APA], 2020)-style statement for a correlation test includes whether you have a significant correlation or not, the direction of that relationship (positive or negative), the Pearson’s r value and p statement. Because we rejected the null hypothesis and we have a significant correlation, we would write “p < .05”:

There was a statistically significant positive relationship between peer victimization and dating violence victimization, r = .97, p < .05.

Summary

Correlation using Pearson’s r can give you information about the relationship between two variables; it can be negative, positive, or zero, and it can also give you information about magnitude (i.e., there is a stronger correlation the closer you are to –1 or 1). Correlation does not imply causation; it simply assesses how the two variables move together.

19

Chapter 19: Linear Regression

In the previous chapter, you saw how to calculate the Pearson’s r correlation hypothesis test. If you have a significant correlation, then you may want to examine that relationship further. Remember, correlation does not imply causation; you simply know there is a relationship between the two variables. So, you may want to move from describing a relationship to something more predictive. For example, you may have a hypothesis about which of these variables is your independent variable (predictor) and which is your dependent variable (outcome).

Linear Regression

The goal of linear regression is to make a prediction, using the line equation ( y = m x + b x (the predictor), we can then estimate the value of y (the outcome). You will be estimating a line to help in making these predictive estimates. You will be estimating a line that best fits your data points.

We will be examining linear regression with two continuous variables; however, regression analyses can be expanded in different ways (e.g., multiple linear regression allows you to examine two or more independent variables to predict a single dependent variable; logistic regression allows you to examine prediction with a binary dependent variable).

Moving From Correlation to Regression

Now that we have established a significant relationship between these variables, we can use regression to make a prediction. We will estimate a line that best minimizes errors of prediction, which are called residuals. The residual is the distance between the estimated line and each data point.

In algebra, we use y = m x + b linear equation. Because we are now estimating a line, in the world of inferential statistics (with inherent room for error), we will use different linear equation notation, as presented in Table 19.2.

Table 19.2. Linear Equation Components and Descriptions

(“y-hat”) Predicted value of your outcome

a

Estimated y-intercept, which is the predicted value of y when x is equal to 0 (i.e., when the line crosses the y-axis).

b

Estimated slope, which represents the average change in y for every 1-unit increase in x. You may see the slope called the rate of change or described as the rise over run (i.e., how much the line goes up or down, and how much the line moves horizontally).

In statistics, you may also see this referred to as your regression coefficient, which quantifies the direction and magnitude of the relationship between the independent and the dependent variable.

x

The predictor variable (independent variable) value.

There are also some additional formulas you’ll need to calculate these components of the linear equation, as described next.

Formula 19.1. Calculating Slope and y-Intercept

Slope formula and description:

b = S P x y S S x

Slope: The slope uses the sum of products of x and y (which you estimated in Part 2 of the Pearson’s r calculations) and the sum of squares for x (your predictor variable; you estimated this in Part 1 of the Pearson’s r calculations).

y-intercept formula and description: 

a = y ¯ − ( b ) x ¯

y-intercept: The y-intercept uses the mean of y ( y ¯ and the mean of x ( x ¯ ), as well as your slope estimate.

b = S P x y S S x

y-Intercept formula and description: 

a = y ¯ − ( b ) x ¯

Our example: 

Slope: 

b = 73 60.9 = 1.20

For every 1-unit increase in childhood stressors, you would predict an estimated 1.20 increase in the anxiety score.

y-intercept: 

a = 17.0 − ( 1.20 ) 5.9 = 9.92

When the number of childhood stressors equals zero, your y value is predicted to be 9.92. This is where the line would cross (or start at) the y-axis.

Now, we have the information we need to write our regression linear equation. 

Formula 19.2. Calculating Predicted y Value using the Linear Equation

Linear equation: 

y ^ = a + b x

Example 19.3. Writing Our Linear Equation

Linear equation: 

y ^ = a + b x

Our example: 

y ^ = 9.92 + 1.20 x

We can use our equation to make predictions about our outcome if we know what our x value is:

y ^ = 9.92 + 1.20 x

For example, if you have another participant who scores an 8 on the childhood stressors assessment, you can use this equation to make a prediction about what their anxiety score will be:

y ^ = 9.92 + 1.20 ( 8 )

y ^ = 19.52

So, if you had a participant score an 8 on the childhood stressors assessment, you would predict their anxiety assessment score to be 19.52.

Our goal with linear regression is to estimate a line (and predictions) that reduces the amount of residual distance between actual and predicted values. You can estimate the amount of residual you have for each of your data points (to see how close each y value is to the estimated y ^

Summary

This chapter introduced the linear regression equation and the ways in which you can use regression analyses to make predictions based on your variables. You may want to continue studying linear regression, for example, by running a hypothesis test to see if you have a significant slope (i.e., is your slope significantly different from a slope of 0?). You may also want to test multiple predictors and see if one or more of these predictors can explain the change in a dependent variable.

20

Chapter 20: Chi-Square Analyses

The last type of inferential statistics that is used to examine relationships is chi-square ( χ 2 chi-square goodness-of-fit test, which focuses on an univariate frequency distribution. There is also a chi-square test for independence, which examines the association between two categorical variables. We will discuss both tests in this chapter.

Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit Test

The chi-square goodness-of-fit test focuses on an univariate frequency distribution for a nominal variable. We can run a hypothesis test, but keep in mind that because you have a nominal variable, you are running a nonparametric analysis. This means that the data do not meet the assumptions (e.g., data are a normal distribution with continuous data) that all of our previous parametric analyses did (e.g., z-test, t-tests, analysis of variance [ANOVA], correlation). However, we can examine distributions of frequencies across nominal categories.

Example: Therapeutic Approaches

You survey 100 social workers on their favorite therapeutic approach. (Read more about evidence-based therapeutic approaches).

This is what you observe:

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy: 35
  • Person-centered therapy: 25
  • Psychodynamic therapy: 10
  • Systemic therapy: 30

You want to test whether there are meaningful differences between categories or whether the difference in the distribution is due to chance. You will test what you observe in comparison to expected values (i.e., equal distribution across categories with N = 100):

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy: 25
  • Person-centered therapy: 25
  • Psychodynamic therapy: 25
  • Systemic therapy: 25

Hypothesis Test for Chi-Square Goodness-of-Fit

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

First, you will write your null and alternative hypotheses about the population chi-square distribution. Your null hypothesis would state that your sample’s distribution fits the expected distribution (i.e., observed frequencies are consistent with expected frequencies). Your alternative hypothesis would state that your sample’s distribution does not fit the expected distribution (i.e., observed frequencies are not consistent with the expected frequencies; at least one category has a different proportion than what would be expected).

You are making inferences about population proportions, so your statements will make reference to probability (p). In our example, we have four categories, so your statements would look like this:

  • Null hypothesis: p 1 = 1 4 , p 2 = 1 4 , p 3 = 1 4 , p 4 = 1 4
  • Alternative hypothesis: At least one of the proportions is not equal to 1 4

You may also see the statements written using “f” for frequencies. In this case, your null hypothesis would state that your observed frequencies are equal to your expected frequencies. Your alternative hypothesis would state that your observed frequencies are not equal to your expected frequencies.

  • Null hypothesis: f o = f e
  • Alternative hypothesis: f o ≠ f e

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? Chi-square goodness-of-fit test
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves examining the frequency distribution of one nominal variable.
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.

A chi-square test uses the chi-square distribution, which changes shape based on its degrees of freedom; the distribution includes only positive numbers, and it is positively skewed in shape. As the degrees of freedom increase, the distribution shape begins to resemble a normal distribution.

    • Your degrees of freedom are calculated by taking the number of categories in your nominal variable and subtracting 1. So, in our example, we have four categories, so 4 – 1 = 3 degrees of freedom. We would then use this to look up our critical value (in Table A.5.). Because all chi-square values are numbers squared, we will only see positive chi-square values, including our critical value.
  • Find your critical value. In our example, χ 2 .

Step 3: Test Statistic Computation

First, you’ll want to find the difference between each category’s observed and expected values (see Table 20.1).

Formula 20.1. Calculating Chi-Square Obtained Value

Formula for χ 2

χ 2 = ∑ ( ( O − E ) 2 E )

Step 4: Make a Decision

Next, you will compare your obtained value (14) to your critical value (7.815). Your obtained value exceeds the critical value, so you would reject the null hypothesis. This means there is a significant difference in what was observed in your frequency distribution compared with what was expected.

APA-Style Write-up

In your American Psychological Association ([APA], 2020)-style write-up, you will include your decision (significant or not significant difference), your degrees of freedom and sample size in parentheses, your obtained value, and your p statement:

There was a significant difference in preferences for these four therapeutic approaches among social workers, χ2(3, N = 100) = 14, p < .05.

Pairwise Comparisons

Like the pairwise comparisons we did after an ANOVA test (see Chapter 17), you can also compare each group to find where the significant difference or differences exists. You can compare each of the groups to each other; because you are doing pairwise comparisons, you will use 1 degree of freedom (2 groups that you are comparing, minus 1) as your critical value (from Table A.5, you see that χ2 =3.841 with alpha = 0.05).

For example, you could test cognitive-behavioral therapy against systemic therapy. To do so, you’ll need to recalculate your proportions because as you now have N = 65 (35 people chose cognitive-behavioral therapy and 30 chose systemic therapy), as shown in Table 20.4.

You will compare your obtained value (0.38) to your critical value (3.841). Your obtained value does not exceed the critical value, so you would fail to reject the null hypothesis. Your APA-style statement would be as follows: 

There was not a significant difference between therapists’ preferences for cognitive-behavioral therapy or systemic therapy, χ2 (1, N = 65) = 0.38, p > .05.

You could then continue testing all your comparisons:

  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy against person-centered therapy
  • Cognitive-behavioral therapy against psychodynamic therapy
  • Person-centered therapy against psychodynamic therapy
  • Person-centered therapy against systemic therapy
  • Psychodynamic therapy against systemic therapy

These pairwise comparisons can help you find exactly where the significant difference or differences exist.

Chi-Square Test of Independence

Next, we will examine the chi-square test of independence, which focuses on bivariate frequency distributions of nominal variables. You can run a hypothesis test, although again, keep in mind that you are running a nonparametric analysis.

Hypothesis Test for Chi-Square Test of Independence

Step 1: Hypothesis Pair

Your null hypothesis would state that there is no association between your two nominal variables–that is, that the percentage of one of your variables is equal in each of the other variables’ groups. Your alternative hypothesis would state that there is an association between your two nominal variables; the percentage of one of your variables is not equal in one or more of the other variables’ groups.

  • Null hypothesis: The percentage of therapists’ preferences for therapeutic approach is equal across therapists’ racial identity. There is not an association between these two variables. (Can also be written as “The two variables are independent.”)
  • Alternative hypothesis: The percentage of therapists’ preferences for therapeutic approach is not equal across therapists’ racial identity. There is an association between these two variables. (Can also be written as “The two variables are not independent.”)

Step 2: Setup for the Test

  • What inferential test are you using? Chi-square test of independence
    • Reasons for selecting this test:
      • Your research question involves examining the frequency distribution of two nominal variables.
  • Set your confidence/alpha: Confidence = .95, and alpha = .05.

To find your degrees of freedom, you will take the number of rows of data you have ( r – 1 ) ( c − 1 ) ( 4 – 1 = 3 ) d f = ( 1 ) ( 3 ) = 3

  • Find your critical value. Using Table A.5, you find that for 3 degrees of freedom, χ2 critical = 7.815.

APA-Style Write-up

In your APA-style write-up, you will include your decision (significant or not significant difference), your degrees of freedom and sample size in parentheses, your obtained value, and your p statement:

There was not a significant association in preferences for these four therapeutic approaches among social workers by racial identity, χ2(3, N = 100) = 1.73, p > .05.

Summary

The chi-square tests presented in this chapter give you an idea of how you can examine univariate and bivariate nominal variables, including associations between two nominal variables using the chi-square test of independence. Chi-square tests are often reported when a cross-tabulation table is presented in reports or papers.

VII

Conclusion

This book provides you with an introduction to statistics, with a focus on applied statistics in social work practice. We reviewed how to calculate descriptive statistics and inferential statistics, both of which can provide evidence for program or intervention impact, inform treatment decisions, or inform policy. These mathematical techniques can be used to organize, summarize, and interpret data, whether you are collecting your own data, reviewing existing data, or reading about other people’s research.

As was stressed in Chapter 1, social workers rely on statistics to make important decisions. Even if you do not calculate statistics of your own in the future, it is essential that you are able to read about statistics and keep up to date on evidence-based practices and scientific literature. Being versed in statistics is in alignment with Council on Social Work Education (CSWE) Core competencies because these skills will make you a stronger advocate and social worker.

Figure C.1. “A Woman in a Pink Shirt Holding a Megaphone” by Lara Jameson, via Pexels, 2021. Pexels license.

From this foundational knowledge of social work statistics, there are many ways to continue expanding your learning. You may take a course in research methods, where you learn different ways to design research studies, collect different types of data (with all different levels of measurement!), learn analytic approaches to qualitative research, or learn how to write and validate your own assessment tools. You may take additional courses in statistics, where you can look at multivariate statistics; there are so many different inferential statistics to learn about and expand your toolbox of how you can approach and test research questions.

There are also courses where you can learn computer software programs that calculate descriptive and inferential statistics for you. With the knowledge you gained in this book, you’ll be informed about where these numbers come from, how to interpret them, and how to write up results in American Psychological Association (APA)-style format. For example, the Data ToolPak in Excel is a free add-on, and it can calculate all of the statistics we learned in this book.

The remainder of this chapter includes summaries of key elements, including concepts, notation, symbols, and equations.

Unit 1: Introduction to Statistics

Tables C.1 and C.2 summarize key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 1.

Table C.1. Unit 1 Concepts

Concept

Definition or Details

Research

Systematic method of inquiring, exploring, examining, or investigating questions, with the aim of discovering new findings, demonstrating impact, advocating for change, solving problems, or advancing theories

Evidence-based practices

Integrating the best research evidence, clinical expertise, and participant and community values

Populations and parameters

A population is an entire set of individuals we are interested in learning about. Numerical values used to summarize data from a population are called parameters.

Samples and statistics

A sample is a subset of individuals from a given population. Numerical values used to summarize data from a sample are called statistics.

Descriptive analyses

Descriptive parameters and statistics are used to organize, summarize, and communicate information about your data.

Inferential statistics

Inferential statistics use samples to draw conclusions about a population using specific tests. Thus, we use inferential statistics with samples.

Scientific method

The process in which we test a research question: (1) Ask a question, (2) conduct background research, (3) generate testable hypotheses, (4) design the study, (5) gather data to test hypotheses, (6) analyze results, and (7) draw conclusions.

Quantitative methods

Methods that use numerical data to examine relationships and differences

Qualitative methods

Methods that often use non-numerical data, such as text or audio from interviews, focus groups, or observations, to explore and examine themes and experiences

Variables

Any observation of a physical attribute, attitude, behavior, characteristic, mood, experience, and so forth, that can take on different values

Univariate statistics

Analyses that summarize numerical information about a single variable

Bivariate statistics

Analyses that examine differences and relationships between two variables

Multivariate statistics

Analyses that examine differences and relationships between three or more variables.

Independent variable

A variable that causes change or affects the other variable; also known as a predictor variable

Dependent variable

A variable that is affected or changed by the independent variable. The dependent variable is what is hypothesized to vary or change depending on the independent variable. Also known as an outcome variable. 

Operationalization

The process of how we measure our variables; translating a variable into measurable terms

Level of measurement

Ways in which the values of a variable are expressed or scaled

Nominal variables (categorical)

Nominal variables are the lowest level of measurement; numerals are assigned to categorize (label) various characteristics or attributes, although these numerals are arbitrary and are simply used to organize the data.

Ordinal variables (categorical)

Ordinal variables organize values with rank ordering (e.g., first, second, etc.). This allows us to classify or organize values again and allows us to put those categories in a particular order.

Interval variables (continuous)

Interval variables classify a variable’s values into order but we also know the interval or distance between values. There is no true zero point, though.

Ratio variables (continuous)

Ratio variables are the highest level of measurement; ratio variable values are used to classify, they go in a particular order, we know the interval between values, and there is a true zero point (i.e., zero represents the absence of what you are measuring).

Distributions and Frequency Distributions

Distributions show us how groups of values are organized, and frequency distributions group together cases with the same values. Tables are useful for displaying frequency distributions.

Figures

Figures are when charts, pictures, or graphs are used to help display and describe data.

Bar charts and pie or donut charts are common figures for categorical variables.

Histograms and frequency polygons are common figures for continuous variables.
Table C.2. Unit 1 Symbols and Equations

Symbol or Equation

Description

N

Total number of participants in a population or sample

n

Subset of participants (e.g., subsample)

Percentage = n N × 100

Percentage calculation

Unit 2: Descriptive, Univariate Parameters and Statistics

Tables C.3–C.5 summarize key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 2.

Table C.3. Unit 2 Concepts

Concept

Definition or Details

Central tendency

A value (or values) that describe the most typical, average, middle, or common value in a data set

Mode

The value or values in a data set that are the most frequently occurring (the most common value). Can be used at all levels of measurement.

Median

The value at the midpoint in an ordered data set (the middle, with the same number of values above and below it). Must have an ordinal level of measurement or higher.

Mean

The value found by calculating the average of a data set (i.e., taking the sum of all values, then dividing by the number of cases or people in your population or sample). Must have an interval or ratio level of measurement.

Variability

A value that describes the dispersion or spread of values around a point of central tendency

Range

Distance separating the highest from the lowest values

Sum of squares

Squared deviation scores (which represent how far each value is from the mean) to measure overall variability

Variance

Another way to measure overall variability, but it accounts for the size of your population or sample, by dividing your sum of squares by N

Standard deviation

Another way to measure overall variability, but it removes squared units (which variance is in squared units). You’ll take the square root of the variance to find the standard deviation.

Normal distribution

Also referred to as the bell-shaped curve because of its shape, the normal distribution is a theoretical distribution. This means that the distribution resulted from mathematical principles rather than actual data. Thus, it provides a visual reference and the key features of how a variable is expected to look (i.e., be distributed). In statistics, we can use this theoretical model and compare our actual data distributions to it; we can approximate it.

Kurtosis

Assesses the “peakedness” of a distribution, which reflects the weight of the distribution tails. A normal distribution has a mesokurtic shape. When a distribution has high levels of kurtosis, it has a leptokurtic shape (more cases in the tails); when a distribution has low levels of kurtosis, it has a platykurtic shape (fewer cases in the tails).

Skew

The extent to which a distribution departs from being symmetrical, as a result of being pulled by outliers on one side of a distribution. A normal distribution has zero skew; positive skew means outliers exist on the right-side of the distribution, so the left-side curve and tail are clustered. Negative skew means outliers exist on the left-side of the distribution, so right-side curve and tail are clustered.

x represents each variable value in your data set.

N represents the number of cases or people in your population or sample.

Unit 3: Standard Normal Distributions and z-Scores

Tables C.6–C.9 summarize key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 3.

Table C.6. Unit 3 Concepts

Concept

Definition or Details

Standard normal distribution

This distribution has a mean of 0 (at the center of the distribution), and a standard deviation of 1 (lines going above and below the mean at the center of the distribution are in increments of 1). Thus, if a z-score is positive, it is above the mean (of 0). If a z-score is negative, it is below the mean (of 0). Thus, you can transform any raw scores into z-scores, plot them on the standard normal distribution, and then easily make comparisons because they are on the same standard scale.

z-score

A standardized score based on a raw score (x), population or sample mean (𝜇 or x̅), and standard deviation (𝜎 or s) that you are comparing it to. A z-score is scaled in terms of standard deviations and is plotted on the standard normal distribution.

Interpreting z-scores (probability and proportion)

The z-score can be further interpreted in terms of probability and proportion; you can use Table A.1 in the Appendix to look up areas between your z-score and the mean, as well as the area beyond your z-score. These areas can be used to answer questions about probability (e.g., what is the probability of scoring higher than a positive z-score?) or the proportion of a population with scores less than a particular z-score.

Percentile scores

Percentage of scores that fall below the observed score

Cut-off scores

With cut-off scores, we start with the percentage we are interested in and work backwards to find the z-score and raw score (x) that are associated with the top or bottom percentage.
Table C.7. Unit 3 Symbols and Notation

Symbol or Notation

Description

x

This is the score that you want to convert.
μ or x ¯

This is the mean of the group you are comparing your participants’ scores to.

σ or s

This is the standard deviation of the group you are comparing your participants’ scores to.

z

Unit 4 covers the calculation of z-scores; they are scaled in terms of standard deviations and are plotted on the standard normal distribution.

 

Table C.8. Unit 3 Formulas for Populations and Samples 
Formulas Population Parameters Sample Statistics
z-score z = ( x − μ ) σ z = ( x − x ¯ ) s
Cutoff score x = z ( σ ) + μ x = z ( s ) + x ¯
Table C.9. Unit 3 Steps for Populations and Samples 
Score Type Steps
Percentile score Step 1: Negative z-score: Look up the area beyond z in Table A.1 to find the proportion of cases that fall below this negative z-score.
Step 2: Positive z-score: Look up the area between the mean and z + .50 to find the proportion of cases that fall below a positive z-score.
Step 3: If a z-score equals 0, that means that it is at the 50th percentile.
Cutoff score Step 1: Start with the percentage or proportion of cases you are interested in working with.
Step 2: Using Table A.1, find the area beyond z that is as close to that proportion as possible.
Step 3: Find the affiliated z-score in column 1 of Table A.1.
Step 4: Plug the values into your equation to solve for x using:
x = z ( σ ) + μ

or

x = z ( s ) + x ¯

Unit 4: Introduction to Inferential Statistics and Hypothesis Testing

Tables C.10–C.12 and Key Takeaways C.1 summarize key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 4.

Table C.10. Unit 4 Concepts
Concept Definition or Details
Inferential statistics Allow us to draw conclusions about populations based on samples randomly selected (i.e., sampled by methods of chance, such as drawing names from a hat) from these populations
Sampling distribution A distribution that results from taking an infinite number of random samples of the same size from the same population. This sampling distribution is used in all inferential statistics.
Central limit theorem Shape: As the sample size increases, the shape of the sampling distribution approximates normality (approximates the normal distribution), which allows us to use statistical analyses based on the normal distribution (see Chapter 7).
Mean: The mean of the sampling distribution equals the mean in the population from which samples were randomly selected.
Variability: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution decreases as the sample size increases; in other words, larger samples lead to more accurate estimates (with less sampling error). We can compute this expected sampling error (also known as the standard error).
Sampling error Difference between our sample statistic and population parameter
Standard error Expected sampling error
Confidence intervals Provide us with a way to assess our level of confidence in representing the population; they can tell us with 95% or 99% confidence that we have represented the population. Thus, confidence intervals give us a range within which a population parameter is located.
One-sample z-test Compares one sample mean to a population mean and standard deviation
Confidence This is the total area of the distribution that is not in the tail or tails of a distribution. Commonly, you’ll see people set their confidence level at 95%, but you can also set it to 99% or another confidence level.
Alpha (α) This is the total area of the distribution that is in the tail or tails of a distribution. Because the alpha and confidence areas add up to 1.00 or 100%, your alpha area would be set at 0.05 or 5%.
Critical value(s) Value that separates your confidence and alpha areas of a distribution.
Probability values (“p values”) Probability values, or “p values,” are computed alphas. When the p value is less than the alpha you set, you reject the null hypothesis.
Probability values, or “p values,” are computed alphas. When the p value is greater than the alpha you set, you fail to reject the null hypothesis.
Type I error This is when you say there is a difference (“reject the null hypothesis”), but there actually isn’t a difference. You may see this referred to as a false positive.
Type II error This is when you say there is no difference (“fail to reject the null hypothesis”), but there actually is a difference. You may see this referred to as a false negative.

 

Key Takeaways C.1. Unit 4: Hypothesis Testing Steps

  1. Hypothesis Pair
    • Null hypothesis, Ho: Statement of no difference
    • Alternative hypothesis, Ha: Statement of difference

  2. Setup for the Test

    • What inferential test are you using?
    • Set your confidence/alpha.
    • Find your critical value(s).

  3. Test Statistic computation

    • Solve for your obtained value.

  4. Make a decision

    • Reject the null hypothesis.
    • Fail to reject the null hypothesis.

Unit 5: Inferential Statistics: Looking at Differences

Tables C.13–C.16 summarize key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 5.

Table C.13. Unit 5 Concepts

Concept

Definition or Details

t distribution

Area of 1.00 under the bell-shaped curve; the mean is still 0 at the center of your distribution. If your sample size is around 100 or greater, the shape of your distribution looks normal. However, if your sample size is smaller (typically less than 100), the shape changes slightly as a function of your degrees of freedom. Thus, t distributions are a family of distributions; each distribution looks slightly different for each different degree of freedom.

Degrees of freedom (df)

The number of observations or values in the data that are free to vary

One-sample t-test

Allows you to compare one sample mean to a population mean (when population standard deviation is unknown and/or you have a small sample)

Independent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences between two independent sample means (when you have a categorical independent variable with two groups and one continuous dependent variable)

Dependent samples t-test

Allows you to compare differences within two dependent sample means (when you have a categorical independent variable with two dependent groups [e.g., time], and one continuous dependent variable)

One-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)

Allows you to examine differences between three or more categories of one independent variable on a continuous dependent variable

Between-groups  variability

Examine differences between the group means for an analysis of variance (ANOVA) test

Within-groups  variability

Examine differences within each group for an ANOVA test

F distribution

Scaled on variance rather than standard deviation like the t distribution and standard normal distribution. Thus, the distribution starts at 0, peaks at 1, and then extends a tail for positive critical and obtained values. The F distribution is a family of distributions, where the characteristics and shape vary according to degrees of freedom.

F (ratio)

The F-obtained value is the ratio of between-groups to within-groups variability. If the ratio is large, then there is more variability between groups, which indicates more of an effect or difference between groups. If the ratio is small, then there is less of a difference, and there is more room for error within a group. If the ratio is 1, then the groups are identical.

Unit 6: Inferential Statistics: Looking at Relationships

Table C.16–C.18 summarizes key concepts, notations, symbols, and equations from Unit 6.

Table C.16. Unit 6 Concepts

Concept

Definition or Details

Correlation

Degree of a linear relationship between two continuous variables. A linear relationship is one that can be described by a straight line. Correlation provides you with an estimate of covariance, which is a measure of how two variables move.

Pearson’s r

Correlation between two continuous variables can be tested using Pearson’s r. This test provides you with a value between −1 and 1.

Positive correlation

(Pearson’s r value between >0 and 1). These variables move in the same direction. This tells you:

  • The variables are moving in the same direction
  • The closer the value is to 1, the stronger the magnitude.
  • A correlation of 1 is a perfect positive correlation.

Negative correlation

(Pearson’s r value between −1 and <0). These variables move in the opposite direction. This tells you:

  • The variables are moving in opposite directions
  • The closer the value is to −1, the stronger the magnitude.
  • A correlation of −1 is a perfect negative correlation.

No correlation

Pearson’s r value of 0, which means that there is no meaningful relationship between the two variables

Correlation does not imply causation

We can see whether the variables move together in the same direction or in opposite directions, but we do not know if one variable is causing the other variable to move in this way.

Linear regression

The goal is to make a prediction, using the line equation (y = mx + b). So, if we know something about x (the predictor), we can then estimate the value of y (the outcome). You will be estimating a line to help in making these predictive estimates. You will be estimating a line that best fits your data points.

Slope

The average change in y for every 1-unit increase in x. You may see the slope called the rate of change or described as the rise over run (i.e., how much the line goes up or down and how much the line moves over horizontally). In statistics, you may also see this referred to as the regression coefficient, which quantifies the direction and magnitude of the relationship between your independent and dependent variables.

y-intercept

The predicted value of y when x is equal to 0 (i.e., when the line crosses the y-axis)

Residual

The distance between the estimated line and each data point

Coefficient of determination

A way to quantify a residual with an r2 value between 0 and 1; the closer to 1 that your r2 is, the better your predictions are (with smaller amounts of residuals). The closer to 0 that your r2 is, the less helpful your predictions are (with more residuals).

Chi-Square (χ2) tests: goodness-of-fit and test for independence

This statistic examines frequency distributions when you have nominal (categorical) data. You can test to see whether there is a significant difference between what you observe and what you would expect in a frequency distribution. There is a chi-square goodness-of-fit test, which focuses on a univariate frequency distribution. There is also a chi-square test for independence, which examines the association between two categorical variables.
