Glossary

Alpha (α)

The total area of the distribution that is in the tail or tails of a distribution.

Alternative hypothesis

Notated as H a

Bar charts

Charts in which the height of the bars conveys the frequency within categories.

Bivariate statistics

Analyses that examine differences and relationships between two variables.

Central limit theorem

Tenets pertain to shape (i.e., as sample size increases, the shape of the sampling distribution of x ¯

Central tendency

The most typical value in a data set; can be found with an average (mean), by finding the middle or midpoint in a data set (median), or by finding the most common value (mode).

Chi-square

Examines frequency distributions when you have nominal (categorical) data.

Chi-square goodness-of-fit test

A test that examines a univariate frequency distribution for a nominal variable.

Chi-square test of independence

Tests bivariate frequency distributions of nominal variables.

Confidence

The total area of the distribution that is not in the tail or tails of a distribution.

Confidence intervals

Give us a range within which the population parameter is located (with 95% or 99% confidence).

Correlation

Degree of the linear relationship between two continuous variables.

Cutoff scores

To find cutoff scores, you start with the percentage you are interested in and work backward to find the z-score and raw score (x) that are associated with the top or bottom percentage.

Dependent samples t-test

Also known as a paired samples t-test; a dependent samples t-test is when you compare two dependent sample means.

Dependent variable

What is affected or changed by the independent variable. The dependent variable is what is hypothesized to vary or change depending on the independent variable. Also known as an outcome variable.

Descriptive Analyses

Descriptive parameters and statistics are used to organize, summarize, and communicate information about your data.

Deviation scores

Tell you how far away each value is from the mean; you can see how little or how much the scores deviate from the mean.

Directional hypothesis

Also referred to as a one-tailed test; you have just one alpha area, or one tail, that you are testing with your hypothesis.

Distributions

Show us how groups of values are organized.

Evidence-based practices

Integrating the best research evidence, clinical expertise, and participant and community values into our work.

Figures

Charts, pictures, or graphs that are used to help display and describe data.

Frequency distributions

Group together cases with the same values.

Histograms

In a histogram, the height of the bar shows the frequency of each category or value of your variable. Because histograms display continuous variables, the bars of the graph are right next to each other, or the bars are touching.

Hypothesis

An informed assumption or prediction about your research question.

Hypothesis testing

A step-by-step process in testing your research hypothesis with an inferential statistics test.

Independent samples t-test

Compares means in two samples, each randomly selected from a different population.

Independent variable

What causes change or affects the other variable. Also known as a predictor variable.

Inferential analyses

Inferential statistics use samples to draw conclusions about a population using specific tests.

Inferential statistics

Allow us to draw conclusions about populations based on samples randomly selected (i.e., sampled by methods of chance, such as drawing names from a hat) from these populations.

Interval

With interval variables, we can classify a variable’s values into order, and we also know the interval or distance between values. The equal, known distances between numbers allow us to add and subtract; however, there is no true zero point (i.e., zero does not represent the absence of what we are measuring) with interval variables.

Kurtosis

Relates to the “peakedness” of a distribution, which reflects the weight of the distribution’s tails.

Leptokurtic shape

When a distribution has high levels of kurtosis.

Level (or scale) of measurement

The ways in which values of a variable are expressed.

Linear regression

The goal is to make a prediction, using the linear equation.

Mean

The value found by calculating the average of a data set (i.e., taking the sum of all values, then dividing by the number of cases or people in your population or sample). Must have an interval or ratio level of measurement.

Median

The value at the midpoint in an ordered data set (the middle).

Mesokurtic shape

Shape of a normal distribution.

Mode

The value or values in a data set that are the most frequently occurring (the most common value[s]).

Multivariate statistics

Analyses that examine differences and relationships between three or more variables.

Needs assessments

Gather or collect data to understand the need for services and support for a population in a service region or setting.

Negative correlation

Pearson’s r value between –1 and <0; these variables move in the opposite direction.

No correlation

Pearson’s r value of 0; no meaningful relationship between the two variables.

Nominal

Numerals are assigned to categorize (label) various characteristics or attributes. These assigned numerals are meaningless or arbitrary and are simply used to organize and summarize information about this variable.

Nonparametric analysis

Data do not meet assumptions (e.g., data are not a normal distribution with continuous data) of parametric analyses.

Normal distribution

Also referred to as the bell-shaped curve because of its shape, the normal distribution is a theoretical distribution. This means that the distribution resulted from mathematical principles rather than actual data. Thus, it provides a visual and the key features of how a variable is expected to look (i.e., be distributed). In statistics, we can use this theoretical model and compare our actual data distributions to it; we can approximate it.

Null hypothesis

Notated as H o

One-sample t-test

Comparing one sample mean to the mean of a population.

Operationalization

Process of translating a variable into measurable terms.

Ordinal

Organizing values with rank ordering. This allows us to classify or organize values again and allows us to put those categories in a particular order.

P values

Probability values that are computed alphas.

Parameters

Numerical values used to summarize data from a population.

Percentile scores

The percentage of scores that fall below the observed score.

Pie or donut charts

Display frequencies of categorical values; the size of the slice conveys the proportion of individuals in a category.

Platykurtic shape

When a distribution has low levels of kurtosis.

Pooled variance t-test

The two population variances are equal.

Population

An entire set of individuals we are interested in learning about.

Positive correlation

Pearson’s r value between >0 and 1; these variables move in the same direction.

Probability

Assess how likely or probable it is that a result you obtain occurred by random chance.

Qualitative methods

Use nonnumerical data, such as text or audio from interviews, focus groups, or observations, to explore and examine themes and experiences.

Quantitative methods

Use numerical data to examine relationships and differences.

Range

A measure of variability that represents the distance separating the highest from the lowest values.

Ratio

With ratio variables, we can use our variable values to classify, they go in a particular order, we know the interval between values, and there is a true zero point (i.e., zero represents the absence of what we are measuring).

Research

A systematic method of inquiring, exploring, examining, or investigating questions, with the aim of discovering new findings, demonstrating impact, advocating for change, solving problems, or advancing theories.

Residual

The distance between the estimated line and each data point.

Sample

A subset of individuals from a given population.

Sampling distribution

A theoretical distribution that results from taking an infinite number of random samples of the same size from the same population.

Sampling error

The difference between our sample statistic and the population parameter.

Scientific method

The process in which we test a research question; includes seven steps: (1) ask a question, (2) conduct background research, (3) generate testable hypotheses, (4) design the study, (5) gather data to test the hypothesis, (6) analyze results, and (7) draw conclusions.

Separate variance t-test or Welch’s t-test

Test that does not assume the population variances are equal.

Skew

The amount to which a distribution departs from being symmetrical as a result of being pulled by outliers on one side of a distribution.

Slope

Represents the average change in y for every 1-unit increase in x.

Standard deviation

A way to measure overall variability; it removes squared units (the unit of variance is squared). You take the square root of the variance to find your standard deviation.

Standard normal distribution

Also called a z distribution; has a mean of 0 (at the center of the distribution) and a standard deviation of 1 (lines going above and below the mean at the center of the distribution are in increments of 1). If a z-score is positive, it is above the mean (of 0). If a z-score is negative, it is below the mean (of 0).

Statistical analyses

Mathematical techniques used to organize, summarize, and interpret numerical data obtained from assessments, reports, research studies, or evaluations.

Statistics

Numerical values used to summarize data from a sample.

Sum of squares

Squared deviation scores (which represent how far each value is from the mean) used to measure overall variability.

T distribution

Looks very similar to the standard normal distribution. Area of 1.00 under the curve; the mean is at 0. If your sample size is around 100 or greater, the shape of your distribution looks normal. The shape changes slightly as a function of the degrees of freedom.

T-test

Allows us to test inferential hypotheses with smaller samples and when we do not know our population standard deviation.

Type I error

When you say there is a difference, but there actually isn’t a difference. Also referred to as a false positive.

Type II error

When you say there is not a difference, but there actually is a difference. Also referred to as a false negative.

Univariate statistics

Analyses that summarize numerical information about a single variable.

Variability

A value that describes the dispersion or spread of values around a point of central tendency.

Variable

Any observation of a physical attribute, attitude, behavior, characteristic, mood, experience, and so forth that can take on different values.

Variance

A way to measure overall variability; it accounts for the size of your population or sample by dividing your sum of squares value by N.

Y-intercept

The predicted value of y when x is equal to 0 (i.e., when the line crosses the y-axis).

Z-score

A standardized score calculated by taking a raw score (x), subtracting the mean of the population or sample you are comparing it to (mu or x ¯
